If someone qualifies and is going abroad she can claim maternity benefits in Canada before leaving or at any Canadian consulate or embassy around the world.
Mr. Speaker, you can see a rather interesting situation occurring here. Suppose a number of couples on CFB Petawawa, CFB Borden, in Halifax, or in Calgary, are posted to Europe. Before they leave, the spouse in house A may find out she is pregnant. So she can make arrangements to collect unemployment insurance for the period after she arrives in Europe.
The next-door neighbour may have four or five children in the family, which is a very expensive operation to run today, and the spouse has to quit her job in Canada, live on one income in Europe, and still raise those children, but she does not qualify for unemployment insurance benefits.
So this situation creates a real dilemma. I do not think it is a very fair way to have been treating the Canadian Armed Forces on this issue over the years. I feel we should be taking a very serious look at this issue again and should be reviewing the legislation accordingly.
We have to understand that jobs are very limited. For example, in Lahr, Germany, there might be a number of jobs at the Canex operation and at all its related facilities. Even teachers who go over find it very difficult to work into the system because, normally, when they get there the positions are already filled for the year and, unless someone becomes sick or must resign for one reason or another, openings do not come up very readily.
We are putting them in a situation where the competitiveness for the few jobs, compared with the large number of personnel and their spouses on the base, results in not a great deal of opportunity for them. It would be very humane for us to take a good look at this issue and let those forces families know that we do appreciate the kind of image they are projecting for Canada because I have always said that our Canadian forces are not only good soldiers, but also professional people, such as nurses, dentists, doctors, engineers, and some very well-trained tradesmen in every occupation. The Canadian Armed Forces are probably one of the biggest training schools we have in Canada, if we look at them in that way.
Private Members' Business
Not only are they good soldiers because of all this, but they are also good diplomats, because they know how to conduct themselves abroad and they give Canada a good image. They are also good politicians because they have to deal with people of many different nationalities. It is their job to try to bridge the gaps and get along with those people and they do it very well. I have always said that our Canadian forces are good diplomats, soldiers, and politicians combined, all rolled up in one ball of wax.
I am making two strong recommendations today, Mr. Speaker, and I know that your heart is in this issue because you have been very close to the forces personnel over the years, yourself. I recommend that we pay unemployment insurance benefits in a normal way to the spouses when they go into areas where they do not presently qualify. Or suppose they do qualify for unemployment insurance, having the required number of weeks, and all their records intact. Suddenly, the other spouse is posted out of the country and they leave.
Why is it not possible for the government and Parliament-I am sure it would be accepted on both sides of the House very readily-to keep all their unemployment insurance records intact during their absence from the country, be it for a year and a half, two years, or three years?
When they return to Canada their unemployment insurance records will still be intact, in the same way as if they had never left the country. Then they will be able to draw UI benefits when they return to Canada and use those as income until such time as they find a job. I think that is a fair solution if the government does not want to change the approach and pay unemployment insurance benefits overseas under the normal process.
The arguments that might arise against this recommendation might include that, first, we cannot afford to do so. We have to remember that the government has considerably increased the contributions for both unemployment insurance clients and the employers. We also have to remember that, under normal conditions, the Government of Canada would not be paying into that unemployment insurance fund nationally. So the government is a shareholder in the unemployment insurance field.

April 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
What about the spouses of business people who go abroad to represent a company, for example? The argument might be made that, if someone is posted to Mexico or Italy on behalf of a Canadian corporation why should their spouse not qualify for the same benefits? Well, perhaps we can look at the same approach, because we are living in a mobile world today.
There is a big movement today on the part of Canadian citizens around the world and we, as Parliament, must continue to update and modernize our legislation to fit those new practices that work their way into the operations of our nation generally, whether public or private.
Of course, we will hear the argument, as we did before the Public Accounts committee when we were studying Public Service 2000 and the foreign service officers came before our committee, as well as others in the Public Service and union groups, stating that they are in the same position. When their spouses go overseas they cannot collect any benefits. So you will hear about all those situations.
Today's motion deals with the Canadian Armed Forces and, because we depend upon the Canadian forces to do excellent work for this country, I think we have a duty to try to make things easier for their family lives. As we know, when people cut down from two incomes to one and go abroad, doing so does not make things easier for them. If they cannot draw unemployment insurance at the same time we are cutting back on their privileges there as well and are not giving them the same opportunity to receive income as people who do not have to fulfil those important duties abroad.
I submit this recommendation to all my colleagues in the House and to the government. I loiow the hon. member for Burlington has had a very soft spot in his heart for this type of issue, as does the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, who has been a distinguished serviceman himself and knows this subject on a very personal basis.
It has been my privilege to work very closely with virtually thousands of Canadian Armed Forces families. So I would ask that the House give this motion some very serious consideration and I hope that we can also look at the motion in a humanitarian manner to try to use it as a
good morale booster for our Canadian forces in showing them that we, as a Parliament, do care about what they are doing, internationally and domestically.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Then I will recognize the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was talking to the hon. member this afternoon and I told him I had put a similar motion down in this House in 1973. It had a little different thrust to it. My concern was that Canadians were overseas on some of our bases, working for Canadian contractors. Unemployment insurance was being deducted from their wages, but they could not collect it.
My point was, if it cannot be collected, do not deduct it. The matter was talked out by a parliamentary secretary who is now a federal court judge. So I will end the story there.
I rise in connection with the motion of the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke. The sense of the motion is that the government should make changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act so that spouses of Canadian military personnel posted overseas would be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
I recognize the validity of the problem the hon. member is addressing in this motion. The service man or service woman is transferred overseas, let us say to Germany, and the spouse who wants to accompany the serving member is forced to give up a job in Canada. That creates problems.
The dilemma, of course, is faced not only by the serving personnel of the armed forces and their spouses, it is also faced by people who work for External Affairs. It is faced by advisors who go overseas on missions for CIDA. It is faced by Canadians who work with international agencies operated by the United Nations. In the private sector it is faced by employees of an increasing number of Canadian businesses that do business abroad.
This is a problem with which we have become familiar, as increasingly greater numbers of families rely on two incomes. Nevertheless, the method proposed by the hon.
April 11, 1991

member for solving this problem is not one which the government can responsibly support.
The most basic difficulty is this. An extension of the unemployment insurance to cover these circumstances would render the program incompatible with the fundamental purpose of unemployment insurance. Unemployment insurance is designed to insure workers in Canada who have lost their jobs so that they can look for employment. It is structured and financed on the basis of certain assumptions.
When one works in the Canadian job market, one insures oneself for loss of work in that job market. Employers and workers pay into a fund to grant protection in these circumstances. If a person decides for one reason or another to live and work in another market, in another country, he or she is no longer covered. In that respect, the Canadian system is the same as the system in other countries. That is the way it works in the U.K., the United States, France, Germany and a multitude of other countries that operate unemployment insurance programs.
The second problem has to do with the basic criteria which apply not only to the spouses of service people, but to everyone who participates in the UI system. The fact that an applicant pays premiums and then loses his or her job does not automatically entitle them to unemployment insurance. One must be eligible and have met two basic conditions.
First, it is necessary to show that the applicant is actively and continuously trying to find another job. It is incumbent upon every person claiming benefits to confirm this on a bi-weekly basis.
Second, if a job does come along, one must be in a position to accept it.
Let us examine each of these requirements in the context of the particular situation referred to in the motion.
In the first case, I would argue that the need for an applicant to show that he or she is looking for work is not only reasonable, it is fair. That could be said because it applies, not just to one group, but everyone who participates in the program.
Private Members' Business
If we are to exercise a responsible degree of control, we need to enforce this basic requirement.
The question that arises is how can someone living in a different country and in a different job market meets this requirement. In the case of Canadian service personnel or his or her spouse posted in the United States, that obstacle can be surmounted.
Since the early 1960s, we have had a reciprocal arrangement with the United States. It allows continued coverage by the UI systems of both countries for the spouses of federal and military personnel serving across their home borders. Control is not a problem in that situation. American UI authorities have agreed to verify that Canadians in their system are in fact looking for work and that work is available. Once that is confirmed, the cheque is issued here in Canada.
Similarly, our Canadian employment centres perform roughly the same function for American workers on this side of the border. The system benefits both countries because there is a substantial exchange of human resources in both directions. It works well because we are neighbouring countries with similar labour markets and we are willing to make arrangements that are easy to administer.
Unfortunately these conditions do not apply to other countries in which Canada has military personnel. We have no such reciprocal arrangements with them. Flow could the spouse of a service man or service woman posted to Germany or Cyprus fulfil the requirement that he or she is looking for work? The machinery for verification just does not exist.
Let me now turn to that second requirement, namely that the applicant for UI is in fact a valid candidate for employment; that he or she can accept work. How do you meet that requirement? The answer is simple; you don't and you can't. In most cases, the wives and husbands of military personnel are not eligible to work in the host economy. They may be eligible to work on Canadian military establishments overseas, but eligibility to work for a foreign employer is limited. Exceptions can be made, work permits may be offered, but it is not automatic and it requires special authorization. It is granted only for selected occupations.
It may be said that we are mostly talking about work on Canadian bases overseas. Let us be realistic, not many

April 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
opportunities exist in that area. A large proportion of the civilian jobs on Canadian military establishments overseas are held by nationals of host countries.
Another basic difficulty also arises. The motion says:
- the government should take the necessary measures in order that
working spouses accompanying military personnel posted outside
Canada may be eligible unemployment insurance benefits.
I do not know precisely what measures the member has in mind. Presumably he is suggesting that we alter the rules so that employment abroad becomes insurable. We know what difficulties we would face on that measure. His other option is to extend the qualifying period.
My time is getting on here. He has 20 minutes and I only have 10. But I want to say there must be reciprocity in any arrangements we make. As far as I know, not a single one of the countries in which we have a military presence, pays UI benefits or anything like them to its own citizens while they are in Canada. An arrangement of this kind would have to be reciprocal and it could not and should not be done on a unilateral basis by Canada.
Let me say this to the hon. member if I could just get his attention for a moment. I think something can be done. I am not sure what it is, but we have to work within the act as it is and I am sure he understands that. There may be some way that we can put something in play within the regulations and, in fact, there is a book UI and You Outside of Canada.
We should look at the whole area and see if there is some way we can come to some arrangement on this. We may have to change some of the regulations in the act, but it is going to take some time.

Mr. Speaker, I have some sympathy for the parliamentary secretary who had to respond to this. It is obvious from the way he spoke that he has a great deal of sympathy for the motion. The fact that he introduced a similar motion some years ago and suggested that maybe there was some way of changing it so that it could be accommodated within the legislation shows that he wants to do something. Yet he was given a script that tells him it is impossible and undesirable and should not be done even if it could be done.
As I listened to the mover of the motion, I could not help but think that perhaps his alternative was a better way of going. The parliamentary secretary talked about the problems of dealing with foreign countries, but the alternative proposed by the member suggested that the spouse who was moving, not because he or she wanted to go, but simply because he or she was following a spouse. It was not their choice.
That is the case certainly with the military services, especially during peacetime. They do not have a choice. They go where they are sent. The same thing would apply to employees or the spouses of employees of external affairs and perhaps even Crown corporations and organizations like that where the individuals concerned are not serving their own personal interests, are not serving the interests of a corporation, a private corporation, or a corporation held in the private sector, but rather they are serving Canadians. They are serving all of us.
For that reason, I think the mover of the motion and the parliamentary secretary feel that Canada should be able to do something. The fact that other countries do not have reciprocal agreements is not reason enough for us not to want to have them.
The mover of the motion suggested, as an alternative, that the spouse who is losing the credits that he or she has accumulated be allowed to carry those forward and when that person returns to Canada, it would be as though they had never left as far as UI is concerned. The time that they had worked would be to their credit. They would be able to draw on whatever credits they had built up and would be able to take advantage of unemployment insurance benefits if they had put in enough time. In that way, they would have something to carry them forward while they were looking for work. I believe it was the mover who said that it is not always easy to find work and certainly that is the case at the present time in Canada.
If a person could carry forward credits, when he or she returned to Canada it would be possible to start from that point in time as though he or she never left Canada. By carrying forward the credits, if work was found right away, so much the better for that person and for the UI fund. If work was not found, it would be something to carry the applicant on while he or she was looking for work. If that person's circumstances had changed to the
April 11, 1991

extent that he or she did not want to look for work, then he or she would not benefit any more than anyone else would.
It seems to me it would, on Canada's part, be playing fair with people who are leaving the country for quite an extended length of time serving Canadians, not serving their own interests or serving the interests of a private corporation.
I would support this motion and urge the parliamentary secretary to carry back to his government the possibility of accommodating the goal of the mover of this motion by using his alternative rather than paying UI benefits abroad.

Mr. Speaker, just for the sake of the people back home listening, the motion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take the necessary measures in order that working spouses accompanying military personnel posted outside Canada may be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
I guess most of us know what that means. It simply means extending benefits to those outside of Canada. With the exception of the United States, we do not recognize benefits outside of this country. In the case of the United States we do for a number of reasons, some of which the parliamentary secretary touched on. The reason that we do recognize that particular situation in the United States is because of a reciprocal agreement between Canada and the United States. The reason for that reciprocal agreement is simply this: There are some similarities between our labour force in Canada and that of the United States; there are similarities in labour laws, there are similarities in many of the other social programs that the Americans have and we have. The close geographical proximity of the two countries makes it a more manageable and a more workable system so that when individuals do receive their lay-off notices, being a Canadian citizen living in the United States, they are eligible.
In relation to our soldiers, our Armed Forces personnel overseas, certainly at no other time in the history of this country since the second world war does the sensitivity of this issue makes us reflect on the current situation. We know the role our Armed Forces have played in recent weeks and we want to ensure that they are given every opportunity, as other Canadians, to enjoy the benefits that we enjoy at home.
Let us go through just some of what the member who proposed this motion mentioned, and attempt to put a
Private Members' Business
little logic into it. We do not disagree with what he is attempting to do. Perhaps, as the parliamentary secretary mentioned, at some point in the future we can accommodate this motion, and we can improve the situation we presently have. But the member mentioned, when putting forward the motion, and I quote him: "Jobs are very scarce in areas like Lahr, Germany, for example, where we do have a number of Canadian troops". That is an argument that none of us can dismiss, because jobs are very scarce for the spouses of military personnel in areas in Germany and other parts of the world. That is a reality we cannot dismiss.
But, in saying that, would a change in the Unemployment Insurance Actrectify a shortage of jobs in a foreign country? I suggest that it would not.
Although the emotion of the particular question is very acceptable, it does not change the circumstance. How we can accommodate that situation on foreign soil is beyond me. Many of the military personnel who are sent to other parts of the world go for three or four year periods, and that certainly goes beyond the qualifying period of unemployment insurance in this country.
If a solution in the short term is found, it does not completely eliminate the problem. Unemployment insurance only lasts for so long and after that the individuals are still in that foreign country in a labour market that is foreign to them.
Just to pose another element into the question, many Canadians who are serving in areas overseas are not eligible to work in those respective communities anyway, because of particular labour practices, questions of legitimacy of some of the workers in relation to their unions, for example, and the licensing of some of the individuals who would like to work in those communities in those foreign countries but for particular reasons cannot.
This motion does not recognize that under certain conditions the Unemployment Insurance Act does take care of Canadians serving abroad, and spouses of Canadians serving abroad. For example, there is no restrictions on the maternity leave element of the Unemployment Insurance Act. People who are serving overseas can plug into that particular aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Maternity leave is very much a part and parcel of our present legislation, so we do not have to improve that side of the question. In relation to that, the adoption elements whereby parents who are adopting a child are given special consideration

April 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
under the unemployment insurance act also apply to individuals and spouses of individuals serving overseas.
Those special benefits under the UI Act are there and have been there, but can we improve what we presently have, as the parliamentary secretary mentioned? I think we can. If you take a look at Europe and the European Economic Community, the closeness of that community and what they are doing, I think we have to take our hats off to them and say they have done a great deal in terms of labour strategy, industrial strategy and trading arrangements between those countries in Europe, but they have not come to grips with the situation which we are addressing here.
Despite some of the progress that countries in Europe have made, they have not overcome all of the hurdles that we are experiencing here today. In time they will. As the global community in a sense gets smaller, our policies sort of parallel each other and we come closer in our methods of doing business and paralleling particular laws and regulations in respective countries, I have to assume that part of that tells me that in fact we are going to make some progress.
The question that is before us is certainly a legitimate question and is one that is near and dear to all of us. Again, going back to my opening statements, if we frame this within the present context of what our military people have done for us in recent weeks, there is no question that improvements can be made, but we have to be very careful as to how we make them.
We cannot isolate one particular problem without addressing another. The arrangements we have made with the United States of America in relation to this perhaps in future years will happen between us and some of the Europeans countries.
The cost of the UI program is borne by all Canadians who are presently working. That is something we have to remember. Every worker in Canada is contributing. Every employer is contributing heavily to this plan. I think it is incumbent upon us to make sure that those dollars are spent well and spent wisely and that they are monitored properly. Presently we do not have a system to monitor a program such as that if it is extended into countries where we do not have the closeness and
harmony as we do with our neighbours to the south at this time. A lot of it has to do with sheer geography.
I am convinced that as communications continue to improve, as does our ability to dialogue with countries across the world, we will in the very near future accommodate the question in the motion put forward by the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by reading the motion so that we can start from the beginning of this very interesting and, I think, timely subject. The hon. member of Parliament for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke has proposed:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should take the necessary measures in order that working spouses accompanying military personnel posted outside Canada may be eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
To me this is a special motion for special people and I want to tell you why I say that.
I said earlier it was timely. If the members present in the House could remember as we stood here and sat here and debated the United Nations motion toward the end of November just before Christmas, I do not think there was any doubts in the minds of anybody here that the men and women who were serving in the gulf at the time and who would be serving over Christmas and beyond were very special people. They were very special people because they were representing our national interest, despite any political differences we may have had about sanctions or whatever. They were representing the interest of their country at a time when all families were together putting their lives, if necessary, on the line in the national interest of this country.
There is nothing more special in the world then that. But there is another special part of the Canadian Forces that, in my mind, relates to the time. If you count the rotations and consider the changes of ships' companies, I am sure we had well over 4,000 Canadians serving in the Persian Gulf if you totalled it all up. They were men and women of different ranks, different services and from every province in Canada working together for one simple Canadian cause, the national interest. They represent a microcosm of Canada and also represent an example that we could all follow in what they are doing, in what they have done and what they will continue to do
April 11, 1991

in the future as long as they wear the uniform of their country.
If somebody would deny this particular motion on the basis that if we do it for one we have to do it for all, I would ask them to remember Christmas of 1990 when they were with their families and the men and women of the Canadian Forces were serving their country away from their families.
The second aspect of this that I think we should consider is that the members of the Armed Forces have already been short-changed by the unemployment insurance business. I do not remember the exact date and I regret I did not have time to check the records, but it was, I believe, in the mid-1980s, about 1985 when those members of the Armed Forces who, having paid into the unemployment insurance fund, at the end of their career in the Canadian Forces, were they not able to find employment, could not draw unemployment insurance. They were able to, previous to this change in regulations, draw unemployment insurance, which was a pretty sensible thing because they spent a lifetime paying into it.
This change removed the opportunity or removed this benefit from those members of the Armed Forces who had paid in as well as the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I recall vividly the disappointment that this had sent through the members of the forces, not only the disappointment, but the disbelief that their government would do this to them. I may say that there are veterans' organizations, including the Canadian Armed Forces Pensioners' Associations and two or three others, which are still trying to get more fairness out of the system by having this aspect of the Unemployment Insurance Act repealed. In fact, it was not a change in the act but a change in the interpretation. I know how tenacious they are and I know that they will continue to do it.
There were two things I heard here that concerned me. The hon. member for Burlington, and I know where his heart is on this particular issue, talked about people who decided to leave the country. I am sure that he would recall that those members of the Armed Forces whose spouses leave with them do not decide to leave the country. They do not have any options.
Private Members' Business
You may say: "Well, why should a spouse of any organization be entitled because of this particular move?" I think it is an acceptable thing today that people in all professions rely on two salaries. When you move to another country and cannot draw that salary, I do not think there is any question that despite any allowances, which seldom makes a difference in the income that people make as a family, that second income is going to be sorely missed.
This, of course, will have an impact on the morale of the people and how well they serve their country. Not that they would serve any less, but in my mind it creates another disappointment. It is the kind of disappointment that I think we can address.
The second objection I heard to this was put forward by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. He suggested that even if you did draw your unemployment insurance for one year, and if you were on a posting for two or three years, then you would run out in two or three years. I am sure he did not expect us to buy that logic. It was a good try, but we are not asking for anything that other Canadians do not get. We are just asking for the consideration of what the Unemployment Insurance Act does for people in Canada, and if a spouse has to move, to be considered essentially as if that move was forced and caused the loss of a job.
Another argument I heard was that it would be difficult to change the Unemployment Insurance Act. Well, we have short memories if we talk about the difficulty in changing the Unemployment Insurance Act. I recall sitting in this House when massive changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, called Bill C-21, were was brought forward. It did not bother the government to change the Unemployment Insurance Act for the things that it wanted, so I say that of the arguments put forward, this was the third very obviously fallacious argument.
It remains a fact of life. In fact, we will be talking about this very shortly when we talk about the changes in the Standing Orders of this House. The privilege of being in government is that basically, within reason, you can do what you set your mind to do. You get flak from the

April 11, 1991
Private Members' Business
opposition and that is what the opposition is for, to keep the government honest.
The argument that you cannot change the Unemployment Insurance Act because it is going to be too difficult or it is going to cause impediments or this, that or the other thing, I do not accept. I think when government decides it wants to do something for any group of people or for organizations or for businesses, then that is what government does. That is why we are in the House of Commons, to debate the things the government wants to do. It is not the opposition that puts forward bills, it is the government that does this. So if we are dealing with principles, and if we are dealing with the logic that these are special considerations for special kinds of people at a special time, then I think the rest of the detail can follow without any difficulty whatsoever.
If one can accept that there should be changes, and if the changes cannot be as traumatic as is put forward by members of the government to actually treat a spouse as if that spouse had lost his or her job, then at least the consideration should be, as an option, that those who qualify for unemployment insurance when they were leaving, by having enough weeks to qualify, would be allowed to keep this status intact while they were out of the country. When they return to Canada, their UI status would continue again as if there had been no interruption.
I think this is fairly simple to achieve. I think the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke mentioned this as an option as he put forward his motion. I think as a minimum that the government should be able to do this.
There were other arguments put forward by members of the government, but I think I covered the major ones. By way of conclusion, I would just say one more time that this is a special consideration for special kinds of people at a special time, and I think because of that, it deserves very special consideration.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Finance and Privatization):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize there are only a few minutes left in the debate, so I will just try to make two or three points.
I would like to compliment the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke for bringing forth the motion. I totally respect the good intentions that moved him to bring forward the motion. However, I do feel there are some very serious problems implied or underlying it that make it impossible, really, for this House to support it.
I have to assume that he was unaware of these when he put the motion forward. Otherwise, one might reasonably question his intent, and I certainly would not do that.
Such a motion if indeed implemented in law would quite frankly violate the Canadian Charter of Rights. It is my understanding of the Canadian Charter that all Canadians have a right to be treated equally before the law.
If there is a Canadian serving abroad in the Armed Forces to whom we are prepared to give benefits that we are not prepared to give Canadians serving abroad in other contexts, be they for the Government of Canada, with CIDA, with the trade missions or whatever or just serving abroad with commercial enterprises, then it seems to me we would definitely subject ourselves to a Charter challenge. It would not likely succeed.
It is important to point out that the disadvantage that accrues to the spouses of the Canadian Armed Forces when they are posted abroad and inevitably lose their employment at home is not a circumstance in which they are singled out.
This is something that happens to anybody if he or she is in a situation where their spouse is transferred abroad and wants to accompany that spouse. That is part of the process. Increasingly in this society, we have married couples in which both are working.
We have to recognize that the unemployment insurance program in Canada is intended to serve the needs of Canadians within the Canadian context and to respond to the labour market in Canada.
Unemployment insurance, by the way, is paid for in Canada by Canadian companies or Canadian companies working abroad. It is the people employed by these Canadian companies, the Canadian government or whatever and their employers who pay the premiums for unemployment insurance.
The idea of unemployment insurance is to protect them in the event of unanticipated job loss or discontinuity in their employment. It is in response to a Canadian circumstance that we have unemployment insurance. If Canadians go abroad, obviously they are taking themselves out of the Canadian marketplace and can hardly
April 11, 1991

reasonably expect themselves to be treated as though they are within the Canadian marketplace.
I believe one of my colleagues has already made the point that we have a reciprocal agreement with the United States which allows Canadians to participate in the unemployment insurance program if they are in either a border situation or, indeed, if they are in the United States.
For example, if a Canadian was posted to the Canadian embassy in Washington, he or she could conceivably continue to draw Canadian unemployment insurance while at the same time checking in through the employment office in the United States. There is a reciprocal arrangement. Of course, he or she would have to be eligible for employment in the United States by having a green card or landed immigrant status, just as the reverse would apply as well.
I think it is instructive to note one improvement that has been made by this government and was made in Bill C-21, which I thought I heard the hon. member for Bona Vista-Trinity-Conception disparaging only a few minutes ago, was the provision that defined just cause to include a person who was forced to leave his or her employment because their spouse had been transferred.
Indeed, the issue is far more complicated than it might initially seem. I think it is important to note that Canadians who are abroad are not necessarily disqualified. Employment and Immigration Canada puts out a very instructive little pamphlet explaining unemployment insurance benefits for which Canadians employed abroad with Canadian companies are eligible such as, for example, maternity benefits or adoption benefits and so on.
I see the clock is winding down, Mr. Speaker, and I want to summarize. I want to compliment the intent of the hon. member but, quite frankly on reflection, he and other members of the House will realize that it is simply not possible to implement the precise change that he proposes.
