Madam Speaker, there is a lot to cover in all of these rules and I do not intend to try to cover the whole area. The one topic among all of them that I want to discuss is the section dealing with committees.
I came to this House after almost 23 years of experience in the provincial House of British Columbia. I am often asked by people in my own constituency which is larger now than it was before, by people here, and by all over: "How do you feel about making the change? What differences have you noticed?" I always reply that the first difference I have really noticed is that in the federal House the committees seem to have some role, some raison d'etre, some function.
That was not generally the case in the provincial House. Once a year in the provincial House we would get together. The selection committee would recommend the names of the people who were going to sit on the various committees. Someone would be designated as the person to call the group together for a meeting. The committee would meet, elect a chairperson, elect a deputy chair and a secretary, and generally with something like 13 out of 15 committees would never meet again until they were reconstituted a year later.
There was nothing that they could do on their own. They could take no initiative. The only time a committee could actually do anything, even hold a meeting, would be if the minister responsible for that area of discussion, assume it was agriculture, moved a motion in the chamber referring some particular topic or question to the committee for study. Once that motion was passed by the House the committee could start holding meetings, but not until then.
There were a couple of exceptions. The public accounts committee, for example, was ready to roll as soon as it was named, as was the one dealing with private members' bills and standing orders. But with every other committee, they never met unless the minister in charge moved a motion in the House.
In the federal House here in Ottawa it is different. That is something I noticed as soon as I came and
something I appreciated. The committees did their own work. They started meeting almost immediately and started looking into whatever committee members thought was worth while, would be in the interest of Parliament, in their own interest of educating themselves as members or in the interest of the House. I appreciate the difference, thought it was very worth while and, as I say, it is always my first comment when I am asked what is the main difference between operating in the legislature in British Columbia and operating in Parliament in Ottawa?
What concerns me about the changes in the rules is the changes that are being made with respect to the operation of committees. They have been working well. It does not mean that the opposition members get their own way. They can bring in minority reports. They can even get those reports printed, which was not the case provincially. Nevertheless, they do hold their meetings. On occasion, even government members will vote with opposition members on something the committee is doing or the committee wants to do. They operate as a separate group and by and large, in my experience, they seem to vote not party line but in the interest of the work of the committee itself, and that is another difference I welcomed.
Some of the people taking part in this debate have expressed the wish that debate in this House could be the same way. Committee members speak individually without keeping to a party line as we in this Chamber seem to. That is the way committees work and I have enjoyed that aspect of my work as a member of different committees, but that too is changing with the way the rules are presented to us now.
The government apparently is not satisfied with the way the committees have been working. They want them to meet less frequently.
They are cutting down on the opportunities for committees to meet. Twenty-eight committees are going to be divided into five envelopes with two committee rooms assigned to each one.
In some cases, there will be six committees in one of these envelopes and in other cases, seven. Seven committees will be fighting for the opportunity to meet in just two committee rooms which cuts down on the opportunities for those committees to meet.
April 11, 1991

Deciding which committee is going to get a committee room will be left to a new committee, the Standing Committee on House Management. That committee is going to have the right to say which two committees in each envelope are going to have the right to meet. They will not be able to meet if they do not get a room. If they get a room, they will meet.
The Standing Committee on House Management will be controlled by government members, as are all committees. This is an important committee. The government will make sure that the committee is following government policy and direction rather than simply leaving things to chance.
When we look at some of the committees, we might wonder whether the Standing Committee on House Management is going to be guided by the interests of the House generally, or by the members. Is it going to be guided by the desires of the government at that particular point in time?
In each of these envelopes, there are two legislative committees. One would expect that in the event there is legislation to be considered by any of the committees in these envelopes then that particular legislative committee is going to have an opportunity to meet.
The government will be anxious to get the legislation through the committee and back into the House. There will be pressure on to get those committees meeting and to get the legislation passed through the committee and back into the House. This will leave five other committees that are waiting for an opportunity to meet in a room that may be assigned.
How often is that going to happen? How will the Standing Committee on House Management, controlled by the government, not be able to select those committees that are working in the interests of the government at that particular time? This means, perhaps, dealing with a subject that the government would like to have dealt with by the committee or, alternatively, avoiding a subject that the government does not want discussed at that time.
It may not want international affairs talked about. If that is the case, this House management committee would make sure that that particular committee did not have a room to meet in. Effectively, it would stop it from meeting. That is not the case now.
Government Orders
Now, there is sometimes a contest for rooms but the active committees do get rooms when they want them.
Beyond that, the legislative committees are going to be restricted to calling witnesses on technical aspects. That is not the case right now. The legislative committee can hear witnesses on any aspect of the work they are doing.
It is an opportunity for the general public, for groups with an axe to grind or for groups that feel its members have particular knowledge of something-whether they have or not. They feel they have. They want to express their opinions, try to have some influence and effect on government policy and legislation. They can make application if the committee agrees, and the committee will meet with them.
The way this reads now, through the changes that are being proposed, it will only be if someone decides that they are dealing with technical aspects only. It is not clear who makes that decision. Is it going to be the chair of the committee? Is it going to be the committee itself under the control of the government members? Is it going to be the House management committee?
What is a technical witness? Is he or she someone who comes from within the ministry or the department who is going to give evidence as to what the legislation was intended to accomplish? Is that what is meant by "technical" witnesses? There is no definition that I am aware of. There might be one somewhere, but none that I am aware of.
It would seem to me that it is cutting down the opportunities for that legislative committee to really look at the legislation. Mr. Speaker, you and I know that on occasion these committees do bring in useful amendments that are accepted by the government. This does happen. Under the new system, if the only witnesses they are allowed to hear are witnesses that are hand-picked by some group outside of the committee and presented to the committee as the ones who are going to be heard, there will be little opportunity to hear, not necessarily contrary views, but any views that are helping to develop legislation that will serve the interests of the people.
It occurs to me that we are going to get to the point where the only way in which legislation can be examined by anyone other than witnesses approved by the government, or some person representing government, will be when it gets to the Senate, the other place. The Senate will still have its committees. The Senate will still have its opportunities to have witnesses of any kind that a committee is prepared to hear. In those Senate commit-

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
tee hearings, as they have done in the past, it will be much more important in the future that they make opportunities for the general public-and I am not talking about everybody coming in-but people other than those designated as "expert witnesses" or "technical witnesses", people with technical ability or knowledge to be heard.
The Senate will be able to go beyond that. They will be the only ones that will be able to, with respect to a legislative committee. Yes, our standing committees will still be able to hear other witnesses. But when it comes to legislation that has been referred to a legislative committee, then one of the principal roles and the principal opportunities of the legislative committee, as I see it, in my rather limited experience in this House, is to serve Parliament and to serve Canada. That will have been lost to it by the change in the rules that will allow that committee to hear only technical witnesses.
As I have said, the definition of that is open. Who is going to select the technical witnesses? Who will they be and will they be picked by that same House management committee that is controlling everything else?
I said I would not be long and I do not intend to be. I wanted to deal only with this matter of committees, and I have tried to explain that too. In my experience, the committees of the House of Commons are serving the House of Commons very well. They are not just serving Parliament itself, but they are serving the people of Canada very well.
While some of the other changes are important and have been dealt with at great length by members in the House from both sides, I do not think there has not been enough attention paid to what is happening to the committees. That is the thing that disturbs me most. There are other things that are important, but the thing that disturbs me most is that the one feature of the House of Commons that I have enjoyed in contrast to my experience in the legislature in B.C., is the way in which the committees serve. The committees' role, their opportunities are going to be cut down. The possibility of them meeting is going to be up to the House management committee controlled by the government. They may not be able to meet at all unless the government
wants them to meet. When they do meet, what they are able to do is going to be curtailed by the fact that they can hear only technical witnesses.
I will leave the rest to my colleagues to deal with. I wanted to deal only with this matter of committees.
We will be voting on the amendments to committees as a separate item, as I understand the breakdown of the vote. I hope the government will decide to take another look at the damage it is doing to the committee system in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to speak on a particular aspect of these rule changes to the Standing Orders, that of Private Members' Business. I believe the changes that have been proposed to Private Members' Business are very good. They are positive changes, but I would urge the government to go even further.
I would like to give a bit of the history of Private Members' Business and talk about the reasons why we might increase the number of items that are made votable and to increase the number of hours of consideration given to Private Members' Business.
In Canada, at the time of Confederation, it was accepted that private member's bills were as important a source of legislation as bills tabled by the government. The rules adopted on December 20, 1867, gave precedence to Private Members' Business on three days of the week and to government business only on two days. From 1867 to 1906 the House operated under a set of rules that permitted fairly broad participation by individual members in all stages of the legislative process. The introduction and discussion of private members' bills consumed a considerable proportion of the House's time and private members' bills constituted a substantial portion of the legislation receiving Royal Assent.
In the early years the government made no serious moves either to increase its control of the House's time or to accelerate the pace at which legislation made its way through the House. Gradually however the time set aside for Private Members' Business started being encroached upon to enable the government to complete its legislative agenda.
April 11, 1991

At first, this was done "by leave of the House", although it became so customary that eventually the rules of the House were changed. During the period 1927 to 1961 numerous changes were made in the rules governing the introduction and discussion of private members' bills. Not only did such bills lose the pre-eminence that they had sometimes enjoyed over government bills during the 19th century, but the opportunities available to introduce and to discuss them were so severely restricted that their utility as a vehicle for initiating legislation was effectively ended.
The growing role and size of government, the increasing complexity of modem legislation, and the fact that much legislation had a financial component, all contributed to the growing pre-eminence of government. As you know, Madam Speaker, private members are prohibited by the Constitution from introducing bills with a financial initiative attached to them. This development was aided by the increasing cohesion of political parties which tended to restrict the activities of individual members. The government's need to use so much of the legislative time available has meant that the time for Private Members' Business has gradually, but inexorably diminished.
In Canada, during the 30 years from 1944 to 1974 only 14 private members' bills were passed, excluding bills to change constituency names.
There are several procedures in the British House of Commons whereby private members may table legislation. The most significant of these is the ballot. At the beginning of each session the names of 20 members are chosen and a priority established. These members are entitled to have their own bills discussed on Fridays which are set aside for Private Members' Business. In the late 1960s a number of very contentious moral issues, capital punishment, abortion, reform of laws respecting homosexuality and so on were successfully dealt with as private members' bills, although in several cases additional time had to be provided by the government.
In Canada, the 1984 Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, the McGrath committee, made a number of recommendations to reorganize Private Members' Business in the House of Commons. Several of these proposals were adopted. A selection process was established whereby 20 private members'
Government Orders
bills and motions were selected by ballot. From these a committee of members, the privileges and elections committee today, designate up to six of these votable.
The government has accepted the committee's recommendation where there would be 10 bills drawn and 10 motions drawn and 3 bills designated votable and 3 motions designated votable. I would call on the government to allow more items designated votable, perhaps 4 or 5 bills could become votable out of 10 and 3 or 4 motions out of 10 could become votable. Each of these votable items can be debated for a maximum of three hours. I would argue that as bills are more important than motions, we might restrict the number of hours that votable motions are debated to two hours.
Mr. Speaker, as you know a number of private members' bills have been passed into law including relatively controversial ones such as Bill C-204, the Non-smokers' Health Act, sponsored by Lynn McDonald. Nevertheless, certain defects have continued or become apparent. I believe we can go a long way to addressing these. Those are: the lack of time and the lack of the number of items being designated votable.
Now, why do private members put forward bills? They often put forward bills that are of particular interest to their constituents or other interest groups. Ideas for these bills arise from the problems dealt with and the complaints received by their offices. We all get a good knowledge of what is going on in government and in our constituencies by interacting with people and helping them solve their problems.
A member may wish to publicize his or her concern with particular issue. Certain members champion or adopt a particular cause or issue or carve out a particular area of specialization on their own. Private members' bills are a way of making the public and other politicians aware of the member's interest or concern.
They are also a means for members to assert their own individuality and sometimes deal with matters differently than their own parties.
Many government members will usually tiy first to see if the government will introduce certain legislation, although in some cases the individual member may not always receive credit for his or her work behind the scenes. The bureaucracy may be opposed to a particular measure, or the government may not have room in its

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
legislative agenda. In such cases, the member may introduce a bill on his or her own.
Private members' bills are often used, especially by opposition parties, to advocate party positions. This can be perfectly acceptable, but there are, at the same time, concerns over the use of private members' bills to bring forward official opposition, or for that matter government policies or businesses.
More importantly, private members' bills are an important source of ideas. They are presented by members who are often reacting to public concern. Government ministers, on the other hand, are often insulated from the public. Many individual members have or develop expertise in particular areas, or by virtue of their contact with voters are made aware of problems in a unique way. Private members are not captive or influenced to the same extent by government departments; while this can deprive them of expert advice, it also can mean that they are more receptive to innovation and public concerns.
Private members' bills are an important alternative source of legislation to government-inspired bills. Sound ideas emanate from the back benches of Parliament. Moreover, since private members are politicians, they are inherently more attuned to public opinion than are civil servants.
Certainly, the government does not have a monopoly on sound ideas. With members of Parliament active as ombudsmen, they may be just as or sometimes more attuned to the popular view of their interest areas than are ministers or public servants.
Government inactivity is often a motivation for private members' bills. Private members' bills provide an important outlet for individual private members. It allows them to leave their own stamp on the legislative process. If the system were changed so as to improve the chance of success of private members' bills, this would help restore the power of Parliament, as well as revitalize the role of individual members.
Private members' bills allow members to act as individuals rather than as part of a team, yet they still can belong to a team. They provide an outlet, and most importantly, encouragement for individual initiative here in the House of Commons. In an effective private member system, there would not be votes along party lines, nor would party Whips try to get their members to vote a particular way. This would mean that it would be up to the bill's proponents to gamer support. This is, of
course, much closer to a true legislative system where individual members vote as they see fit on individual issues.
Many voters would be very proud of a member who managed to sponsor legislation successfully.
No matter what changes are made to the procedure rules governing Private Members' Business, it is essential that they be accompanied by changes in attitudes. Governments have to stop feeling threatened by an individual member's initiative. They must stop feeling threatened by bills that may not accord perfectly with their own legislative platform. The same is true, perhaps even more so, of bureaucracies that often hinder and thwart private members, consciously or not. Governments and parties have to sincerely allow members a free rein on private members' bills, not insisting on party lines.
Members themselves have to change. They have to be responsible for tabling bills and to avoid silly, petty and poorly drafted ones. If members only tabled bills that they seriously felt should become law, it would have an effect on the seriousness with which all private members' bills are taken. Members also have to make more of an effort to attend and participate in Private Members' Business.
The biggest problem facing private members' bills is lack of time. Every session, hundreds of private members' bills are introduced but only a few are selected by ballot and not enough of them are given enough time to be debated. Once again I call upon the government to allocate one or two more hours a week or consider alternative schemes to increase the number of hours of consideration given to Private Members' Business.
One alternative would be to have two half-days during the week set aside for Private Members' Business. It is conceivable that two morning sittings could be created to deal with Private Members' Business. The advantage of this idea is that it would minimize the disruption of existing House business and time. As we know, an hour here and an hour there prevents real continuity in discussing Private Members' Business.
Of course reform of Private Members' Business is part of a larger issue, the issue that we are discussing tonight, the general reform of the House of Commons, increasing the effectiveness of Parliament and of members of
April 11, 1991

Parliament, enhancing the role of individual members and eroding the dominant role of party discipline.
The power and clout of private members cannot be legislated. It is possible to create opportunities to bring forward their concerns in the form of private members' bills, but much will depend on how they choose their issues, develop expertise, and use the system.
The attitudes of all members of Parliament and of the government will also determine whether the system succeeds or fails. The quality of private members' bills has to improve if there is a real possibility that they might become law and not form a pretext for debate.
There is some evidence that this has happened since 1985 when the McGrath commission reforms were instituted. I must compliment the Prime Minister and cabinet of the day for accepting many of those recommendations, for they have worked extraordinarily well.
Members of Parliament fulfil an important ombudsman role representing their constituents to the federal government. In doing so, they often become aware of areas that need to be addressed or reformed before the government does.
Private members' bills are a way for ordinary members to take advantage of the opportunities afforded them to initiate changes.
Writing in 1974, a newspaper columnist said: "Unless you subscribe to the quaint notion that the only people in Ottawa who are capable of thinking are those that inhabit the Treasury benches, you have to be concerned about the short shrift given private members' bills. It is one more argument for the real reform of the parliamentary procedure".
I think the rules of the House of Commons which have been presented are fine rules. I especially would applaud the government for accepting the recommendations given to it by the privileges and elections committee concerning Private Members' Business. I would encourage it to go that one step further in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I bring an official opposition perspective to this issue, and I do not apologize for that one little bit. Let me
Government Orders
explain. The premise of these rule changes is to limit debate, choke off debate. In the government's view if you delay legislation you make this House, this institution, more inefficient. In other words, it construes delay as inefficiency: "Delay is inefficiency".
Delay in this particular institution is not necessarily inefficiency. In fact, it is an absolutely vital part of the democratic process that is played out within these four walls.
When an issue comes to the floor of the House time must be given to have that issue percolate, to give people an opportunity to express themselves, to arouse the public. All of that takes time. Yet, those people on that side of the House would like us to believe that is delay or inefficiency and that the best way to pursue the political process, to pass legislation, is to do it in a great hurry: "Let us have no delay because that would be inefficient".
They are wrong. The role of the opposition is very vital to the democratic process. Believe it or not, our job which is much different from the job of those people over there is equally important. We have to have our time to do our job as they have to have time to do their job.
Speaking of delay and inefficiency, I suppose if we wanted to include cost effectiveness in efficiency it would certainly be more cost effective if I did not go home every weekend, if I did not get on the iron bird every Friday and go home. I would certainly save the taxpayer several hundred dollars a week. I guess, according to the thinking of some people, that certainly would be cost effective. But, would it really be good politics? Would it be good representation if I just sort of hunkered down here and I went home only once every four weeks or every three weeks?
The fact of the matter is that when you are in public life not only do you have to be here debating issues and taking part in the legislative process, but you also have to be back home. You have to be with your people, you have to mingle with your people, you have to be seen by your people, you have to be touched by your people. It is all part and parcel of the democratic process. It is very

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
important. It is not necessarily the most efficient thing in the world, but it is a vital part of democracy.
I know that when I look at this package of changes I look at it rather cynically. I really wonder whether we would have this package of changes before us today if the government were not low in the polls, if it were not sitting at 15 per cent, 16 per cent, or 17 per cent in the polls. My guess is that if government members were riding high these changes would not be made or these changes would not be proposed. I gather they believe that the only way to political salvation is to shut this place down, rob the opposition of a political platform, and go home to see if it can find their political salvation. I think they are wrong on two counts. They are wrong on this package of changes and there is no political salvation for them. They are beyond redemption.
Let us look at the amount of time we devoted in debate to the goods and services tax.
I pulled out this legislative document, Status of Bills and Motions, and what does it show? It shows that when it came to Bill-62, the GST legislation, debate at second reading was on January 29, 30, 31, February 5, 6 and 7, 1990.
It seems to me, according to my arithmetic, six days for the GST at second reading. Then there was a debate at report stage on April 3 and April 9; two more days. There was a time allocation debate because this government is very prone to time allocation and of course closure. On the time allocation debate two more days, April 4 and 5, were devoted to that. Then there was concurrence at report stage on April 9,1990. Then there was debate at third reading on April 10.
I have added it up and it looks to me as if there were about 12 days of debate in the House devoted to the GST. It seems to me that this government is saying that is too much time.
The GST, when it comes to tax legislation, was a watershed for this country. We had never had this kind of a tax in the country before. In this House of Commons we spent about 12 days debating. Is that too much? I do not think so, yet this government is saying: "That is too much. That is inefficient. That is delay. We have to limit debate".
As one of the previous speakers pointed out, we now face the irony that there will be more ventilation of an issue in the unelected other place than there will be
here. Does that make sense? For the life of me, I cannot understand that.
I also want to touch on this matter of limiting witnesses before legislative committees to what is going to be called technical witnesses. There is a presupposition in that. There is a presupposition that the principle of whatever legislation is being debated, whatever legislation is going before the legislative committee, has already been fully explored some place else, presumably before a standing committee, so why would we want to go through the principle again or to debate the principle again? "Let us just sort of tinker with some technical aspects of a bill and we will leave that to the legislative committee". Does that make sense?
What guarantee is there that when a bill goes before a legislative committee the principle has been fully explored? Is there any guarantee that this matter would have been dealt with, particularly its principles, at the standing committee or elsewhere? I do not think so. It is a sham, but this package of changes is just another example of the erosion of the erosion of our democratic rights.
I want to enter a little positive comment here. There is a provision in this package at a certain point-I think it is after six or eight hours of debate-to reduce speeches to 10 minutes. I do not think it is a bad idea at all. Maybe it is because it is because of my journalistic background or maybe it is because of my broadcasting background, but I would submit that in a majority of cases if you cannot say it in 10 minutes you probably will never say it.
I would think that after six or eight hours there is not going to be anything lost to the public if speeches are limited to 10 minutes.
I want to touch on a couple of omissions; omissions not commissions. First I want to touch on free votes because we do not have many free votes in this House. We do not have enough free votes in this House and this package of changes is not going to help the situation at all.
People out there for better or for worse-and I happen to think it is for better-want to give their public representative, their members of Parliament, a greater role and a bigger voice in this House. What they are really saying to the political parties and to all of us is that party discipline has gone too far, that party discipline is excessive. The pendulum has swung too far in the direction of party discipline. That pendulum has to be pulled back to give members of Parliament more individ-
April 11, 1991

ual expression, particularly when it comes to sensitive regional issues.
Constituents are not stupid. The voter is rather sophisticated. Voters know that parties must stand for something, that parties cannot go in every direction on every issue, that there is many times, perhaps a majority of times, when a party has to speak with one voice. I will just pick one example. When it comes to something as fundamental in a government program as a budget, the governing party in that particular case must speak with one voice for better or for worse.
There has got to be some elasticity in the system, some room for the parties to speak with one voice, but also room for members of Parliement to speak with their particular voices, voices that represent a particular point of view of a particular region of the country.
What is happening now is that members are being asked to be nothing more than puppets. I do not think that is what we are supposed to be. After all, this is supposed to be the highest court in the land.
I think there is something that members have to look at when we ask for the right for free votes. We are not asking to defeat the government on each and every occasion that we want a free vote. All we want to do is to say that we do not like a particular piece of legislation, take it back, redraft it, improve it, and then return it to the House. We are not asking to defeat the government, to kick the cabinet out, to cause an unnecessary election or anything like that. All we are asking is for us to focus on a particularly egregious, bad piece of legislation; to send it back to the shop and fix it up. I do not think that is too much to ask for. I really do not think that is too much to ask.
I want to touch on the proposal of three weeks on and one week off. A part of it is appealing. Certainly that one week off is simply off from this place. It is certainly not off from work. I can assure you, Madam Speaker, that if it goes through I will be spending the so-called week off in my riding and in my riding office. I am sure I will work just as hard during that week off as when I am here for the three weeks.
My concern, though, is that unless we do a very good educational job of explaining what it is all about-and politicians tend not to be good at that-people are going

to look at it cynically. They are going to say to themselves and to us: "Oh, it is just a way of reducing your workload. It is a way of giving yourself another break, another holiday". That bothers me because we are in low enough esteem now.
I am also afraid that this approach of three weeks on and one off from the House will be abused politically, that House leaders, particularly on the government side, will do all kinds of stage managing of sensitive issues around this provision of three on and one off. I can just imagine the government thinking: "How could we perhaps introduce something that is unpopular and is going to cause a lot of flack for the next few days? Maybe we will introduce it just as we are shutting the House down for a week".
You see, there is even cynicism in me, as there is among voters. That worries me, it worries me a lot, because if we politicians are not thought of in a good light, nor will this institution itself. In other words, as we go so goes this institution.
There is also the matter of the televising of House committees. A good idea, Madam Speaker, a very good idea. I said this the other day and I want to repeat it here. If we come to the televising of House committees, I want no part as a parliamentarian, and I don't want to see any other parliamentarian either on this side of the House or that side of the House, deciding which committee is going to be covered with the television camera, be it a permanently installed television camera or one that is hand-held and moves around the committee room. That must be decided by the media and the media alone.
I do not tell the Toronto Globe and Mail, the Toronto Star, the Winnipeg Free Press or any other newspaper or any other publication in this country which committee meeting they are going to cover. They have to decide what is in the public interest. They have to decide what is news and what is not news on a particular day. That is not my decision, that is not the business of the government, and it is not the business of this side of the House.
I know that there is a predisposition in this House that would give some politician the power to decide which committee is going to be covered by television and which committee is not. If we go down that road, that will open

up an unbelievable can of worms. That is a Pandora's box, and we cannot allow ourselves to fall into that trap.
The media is far from perfect. The media makes mistakes every day. But I would rather, in this particular instance, have the media make those mistakes, for better or for worse. That is not our business.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I want to touch just briefly on legislative planning.
The way we conduct business in this House very often does not make any sense. It does not matter which party is in power, it seems to be the same old way. That old way is always keep the opposition guessing, keep the opposition off balance, and if we can give the opposition a matter of just hours' notice about the next piece of legislation to be debated, well, that is well and good for the government.
As I said at the beginning of this speech, the opposition has an important, vital role to play in this democratic process in this House.
Yes, we are adversaries, but there has to be a team approach. We need to have our resources and our time to think through legislation so that when it comes to debating, we know what we are dealing with.
I would like to see much more legislative planning in this House.

Madam Speaker, I represent a riding at the far outpost of the empire, North Vancouver. There are many of us in this House who represent ridings as far away.
Let me describe how I get here. When I leave my home, it takes a good 40 minutes to get to the airport. If I want to catch a plane, I had better be there 40 minutes to an hour ahead of time. I am already into my day with an hour and a half to two hours. To fly from Vancouver to here is a minimum of a full five hours. Then, of course, there is the extra approximately 40 minutes to get downtown from the Ottawa airport and to the House of Commons.
When I come to Ottawa, I have already spent seven or eight hours just to get here. That procedure is reversed when I go back to my riding. I am not the worst off by any stretch of the imagination.
Those people from the interior of British Columbia have to oftentimes overnight in Vancouver and fly from one to three hours the next morning to get back to the voters who elected them. The same thing is true to a certain extent in the maritimes and Newfoundland.
For that reason, I am veiy highly in favour of three weeks sitting and one week off from here. The one week off from here is important for several reasons. What a lot of people in this part of the world forget is that the Rocky Mountains are much more than a geographic barrier. They are a mental barrier as well.
I find that the minute I start thinking what I read in The Toronto Star, The Ottawa Citizen or the Montreal Gazette is important, it is time I went back to British Columbia to find out what the real people are thinking and concerned about.
Believe it or not, the people in this country do not all agree with the Montreal-Toronto-Ottawa access. What these regions consider important is not necessarily important in the other regions of the country. In many cases, it has no bearing at all on that thinking.
Can I find that thinking out, sitting in Ottawa? There is no way. We have to go home and spend time with our people.
I have not been able to accept a speaking engagement on a TUesday or Wednesday night in years. The reason, of course, is that costs me practically a week here. No matter how I slice it, it is a day to get here.
If I take an early morning plane, then I can make it here by five o'clock or 5.30 in the afternoon when the business day is over. If I take an afternoon plane, I am here very late at night. If I take the "Red Eye" out of Vancouver at eleven o'clock or twelve o'clock at night, I may get to Ottawa by nine o'clock the next morning. Believe me, my mind is still exhausted over Saskatchewan. I may be here physically, but not in the best mental shape.
No matter how it is sliced, if we come from the far outpost of empire, it is a difficult thing coming here, doing our work and staying in touch with our constituents. That is why three weeks here and one week off will make a tremendous difference.
April 11, 1991

There are also the time changes involved. There are three hours difference between here and the west coast. I would recite a bit of an antidote.
When the Pope was in North America, his doctor made the statement that for every time zone change of an hour the Pope went through, generally speaking it took the average person at least two days for their biological clock to adjust to that time change.
When I read that, I started thinking about my travel schedule over the previous six months and I came to the conclusion that if I stopped flying immediately, by 1995 my biological clock would be back in the proper rhythm. Unfortunately, it does not happen that way. It is a very difficult thing for members from a long distance away. I am not the only one. If you have a tight little Winnipeg riding, that is fine. You can take about a two hour flight and you are home in your riding. If you are from Montreal, one hour. No wonder you have no sense or understanding of what it means for those members who are a long distance away.
I have heard a good many insensitive speeches in the last three days on this subject. Most of them demonstrated a total lack of understanding of what a good many members go through in terms of doing their job here, representing their people, as I said, at the far outpost of the empire.
I heard some rather cynical speeches, I thought, from some NDP members. They have been doing the three and one for over a year now. Just check them any day and you will find out that about one third of them are away visiting their ridings for that week. To hear somebody be opposed to this one week in four off is simply not fair.
I can think of a great many very terrible movies I have watched at midnight in the city of Ottawa, having got off a plane, got home and it is really only nine o'clock at night west coast time. I wish they had better movies in Ottawa, really, particularly late night ones.
In any event, that is part of the story. The real part of it is the fact that that week off is extremely important to all members if they only knew it. Get out in your ridings, meet your people, be available for speeches, breakfasts or whatever. What happens, of course, is your constituents will very rapidly get to know when you are in town.

They do this, I might add, in Australia. The Australian members have found that after a week at home they come back to Canberra to rest up because everybody in the riding knows you are there, knows you are going to be home for the week, so there are breakfasts, luncheons, dinners. They plan their events around when their member is definitely going to be in the riding. We cannot do that now, but with the three weeks on and the one week off, we will be able to do it. It will be better for all of us, particularly those who come a long way.
Oftentimes, I feel sorry for myself on the plane until I think of some of my colleagues. There are places in Saskatchewan you cannot get to from here, and they have members. Some of the members from Manitoba fly into Winnipeg and then get into an automobile and drive for two or three hours to get home. Try and do that on a Friday night, spend Saturday and part of Sunday at home and then drive three hours back to the Winnipeg airport and try to get to Ottawa.
That one week off in four, I think, is necessary for the health of the country, for the health of the members and also to give the public a real chance to get at their member.
I would dispute what the previous member said about the government attempting to bring in nasty little bits of legislation two days before the week off. I do not think it is going to happen. If it does, it means every member goes back to their riding and will get the fallout from that legislation in their face when they are there and have to explain it. So that does not matter. But a week in four to spend in your riding is particularly important to anyone who has a ridiculous travel schedule to get between Ottawa and their riding.
The only other point I want to make in my particular remarks on the bill is that I am highly in favour of the new committee system for these reasons. I have chaired enough committees here with enough members over the years. One the greatest faults of the whole thing is that so often, in order to make a quorum or to cany on your committee business, you get a stranger who is put on that committee. He does not know the background of the committee. He does not know what has been discussed and, invariably the floaters, as I would call them, are the ones who want to take up most of the time uselessly talking about things they know nothing about. With the new committee system you will have groupings of members. If you are interested in the finance envelope and all

those committees, you will become knowledgeable in each one of those areas and will be of use to a number of committees within that particular envelope. The same will happen with the social services committees.
In that sense I am highly in favour of it because it means more knowledgeable members of Parliament dealing with issues with which they are concerned.
Frankly, there are some other things on which I could agree with the opposition. I find it offensive that the House leaders of all parties have reserved so much power and responsibility to themselves. I do not agree with that. It should be spread out to committee chairman and private members to a much larger extent. First of all, I do not think it is necessary and I do not think it is healthy.
However, I would do almost anything to get that week in four home in my riding, to have an opportunity to take speaking dates when everyone knows you would be there and when there would be a full week, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Monday to conduct business in the riding which many members from way out of town now have difficulty in doing.
For those reasons I am going to be voting for these rule changes and with heartfelt thanks for the changes that are being made. They are all very worth while. For those members with their tight little ridings close to Ottawa, fie on you. Those of us from the far outposts of empire deserve that week off.

Madam Speaker, I am gratified to be given the opportunity to say a few words in terms of the rule changes. I would like to preface my remarks by simply having a complimentary word for our House leader, the member of Parliament for Cape Breton-East Richmond who put forward in response to the government House leader in a very brilliant and articulate way this past Monday, in a speech close to an hour and a half to two hours, trying on our behalf and for the benefit of Canadians to dissect a number of the rule changes that are being proposed. I know that all of the members of our caucus are very appreciative of his efforts and those members of our caucus who assist the House leader such as the hon. member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands.
I would basically like to structure my words in the time allotted to me in three ways. First, to touch very briefly on the full question of closure which I find ironic given the context of the debate this evening. Second, the timing of the proposed rule changes themselves. Third, obviously a few comments on the actual changes that are being contemplated.
On the first aspect I mention that I found it very ironic for closure to be ushered in during a debate about rule changes, rule changes that purport to give greater relevance, greater significance to both this Chamber and to individual members of Parliament. At the same time we have a government that has used closure a record number of times, but becoming much more cold about the whole situation as it introduces closure on the very time that members of Parliament are debating how we can make this place and members in this place function better on behalf of the country and on behalf of Canadians.
I believe if the Chamber is to be made more accountable, if members of Parliament are to be given greater latitude, greater authority and greater flexibility with which to discharge their responsibilities, it would seem to me that their constituents would win if we did not always have the club that has been known in parliamentary language as "parliamentary closure". This is a very fancy way of abruptly closing and choking debate when debate can foster new ideas in new directions. So I find it very ironic that, while we are trying to improve the lot of the House of Commons, closure is being allocated on the other end.
The second aspect-and I say this in a non-partisan way, as a member of this place-is that I find the timing of this debate to be circumspect, to say the least. If I was a member of the Canadian community looking on, by my parliamentary channel, I would see a House of Commons seized by parliamentary rule changes and the debate herein.
I find the timing ill-advised because the country is currently wrapped in what can best be described as a crisis on two tracks, one being the economic track and the other being national unity. We know the situation with respect to the economy, wherever Canadians live.
April 11, 1991

We know that close to 1.5 million people are unemployed; we know plants have been closing; we know de Havilland is being sold, and we know there is double-digit unemployment in my own city of Toronto, which happens to be the heartland of Ontario and the capital of the manufacturing industrial heartland of Canada.
Canadians are in trouble and Canadians are hurting; small businesses are either downsizing, going bankrupt, or going south of the border; Canadians are looking to this government and to this Parliament to inspire a nation, to try to stimulate an economy, and to collectively try to pull ourselves out of the economic pit we find ourselves in.
Instead, we are engaged in what some Canadians are suggesting is a navel-gazing exercise. As important as it is to be reforming this place with a view of hopefully improving it, at the time, be it on the economic front and on a national unity front, when we have one province contemplating whether it wishes to leave the Canadian family, other parts of the country are wishing-in to the Constitution, and Canadians of neither English nor French background want to be encompassed by the debate, we are contemplating rule changes.
The changes are very distant from the causes that are gripping Canadians today and are very far removed from the malaise in which Canadians find themselves. I am sure the changes will certainly fuel the cynicism in which Canadians all too often hold this place and the members that occupy it.
To make matters worse, not only are we debating proposed rule changes at a time when the country is going through one of its toughest times since Confederation, but as soon as we are finished the debate on rule changes, rather than having the expectation of then getting on with the business of Canada, this House is going to adjourn, as proposed by this government, which will close the lights in this Parliament.
On the one hand, Canadians see a Parliament engaged in itself, rather than engaged in the business of removing Canada from this economic and constitutional malaise. Then, of course, after we have finished the business of rule debates and rule changes, we will close Parliament on the excuse that the government has to get ready for
Government Orders
the Throne Speech, which will not be delivered until the 13th, 14th, or 15th of May.
So it is no wonder that Canadians would view this debate as being very much ill advised in terms of timing. I would share that commitment. As much as I have a commitment to improving this place, I have to question whether the timing of this particular debate could not have waited until the issues of the nation were better resolved and whether our forces and energies as members of Parliament would then have been better focused on addressing the issues that are involving Canadians from one coast to the other coast to the other coast.
The third issue on which I would like to spend a few minutes relates to the actual changes and can be divided into three areas. Firstly, the new parliamentary timetable that is being advocated; secondly, the revised committee structure; and, thirdly, the technical orientation.
I think the latter two are of somewhat more of a technical orientation and I have the biggest concern, as an individual member of Parliament, with respect to the new timetable. That new timetable would suggest that the annual sittings of the House would be reduced from 175 sitting days to 135. Notwithstanding the fact that some of those sitting days will then be increased by an hour or so to make up for some of that loss, there is still a House of Commons sitting for less hours overall, over the long-term.
We can say quite rightly and quite legitimately that we need to spend time in our ridings and that we need to be with our constituents and responding to them. I would agree with that and I think there needs to be the time for the Members of Parliament to balance the two communities: the one in Ottawa where this Parliament is our factory and in the riding, which also happens to be a workplace of utmost significance.
I believe that when this House is closed we remove a forum that has been vital for Canadians. We recall the summer that just went by during which we had the situation of Oka and during which the situation in the Gulf intensified, and this House of Commons was closed. There was no apparatus for Canadians to look into these issues, beyond the press releases that were issued by the government and the Prime Minister of the day.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
I recall during that summer when Canadians were asking why Parliament was not open for business then, of all occasions, when it had been brought back a few summers ago on such flimsy excuses as a number of people coming in on the east coast, as one illustration, or as dealing with the Correctional Service. However, when there was a true and real emergency during a crisis, this Parliament was not open.
Therefore, I would lean towards having this place be in operation more often, be more alive, and be in closer concert on the television set in the living rooms of Canadians than having this place closed, thereby removing an outlet that is the forum and the centrepiece for parliamentary democracy in this country; a democracy that people in other countries are dying and starving for.
The other aspect of the parliamentary timetable is that of the 25 allotted supply days would be removed from the opposition. That is a fancy way of saying that there would be less days when the opposition dictates the agenda of the parliamentary day.
That reduction erodes the accountability portion of an opposition. We on this side are not arguing in a purely opposition mode because we know that one day very soon we will be on the other side of the Speaker, in the government benches, and the members on that side will have their roles reversed. So we are trying to speak to the traditions of an opposition in a democracy and the democracy of any country is only as strong as the rights accorded to its opposition. When the rights of the opposition are eroded so is the definition and power of the word democracy.
Therefore, why have fewer opposition days in which the opposition can dictate the agenda for a change.
I have been in the House for six years. I have lost every single vote in the House of Commons. I accept that. The government has a parliamentary majority and I accept that.
But it is not only important who wins the votes, but who wins the debate, has the force of debate, has the force of right on one side, has the ideas, has the clarity, and has the convictions. Therefore, votes are one thing, but debates are a very different subject. Therefore, I oppose quite strenuously the attempt to remove the ability for of opposition on behalf of Canadians to set the parliamentary agenda on any day against a parliamentary government-in this case, a majority government-that
has all the power, all the clout, and all the tools at its disposition.
I would also suggest that two out of the eight Throne Speech debate days be removed. Now the government says that the day of the Throne Speech is one of the most important days in any parliamentary calendar. It provides political inspiration to the government and the party and is intended to provide political inspiration and leadership to a country. The Throne Speech supposedly ushers in "a new agenda". Therefore, is it not logical that, if the government attaches such importance to an undertaking in a Throne Speech, this House, this chamber and its opposition should be accorded the fullest possible time in which to try to explore important undertaking on behalf of Canadians?
It seems illogical, on the one hand, for a government to adjourn for a month to prepare a Throne Speech and to then suggest in its proposed rule changes that there ought to be less debate surrounding one of the most important initiatives a government can take in the parliamentary agenda.
The proposal also goes on to say that two out of the six budget days ought to be removed. Once again, the introduction of a budget is another centrepiece of any government program and of this chamber, of media, and for a country, in terms of the fiscal and monetary policies that will be dictating its course, for not only months but years to come.
Therefore, if a budget is that crucial to the livelihood of a country and its people, why not provide this chamber and the opposition of the day, whoever is in that unfortunate position, the opportunity to try to account again for the parliamentary program, in a budgetary sense, of that government.
It seems to me that we have a contradiction when a government flags the important days of a budget and a parliamentary Throne Speech, then at the same time tries to advocate greater relevance for this place by removing the debate surrounding these important initiatives.
The proposal also talks about limiting a Member of Parliament's speech and cutting it in half after a number of hours. I suppose there are two schools of thought. One is to try to move the debate on. On the other hand, if Members of Parliament are to occupy a more relevant role in this chamber and are to try to be somebodies in
April 11, 1991

this chamber, then cutting one's time in half is not going to do it.
If a Member of Parliament wishes to eloquently discuss an issue affecting one's riding, one's country, or one's Parliament, then 10 minutes- although it is true, Madam Speaker, that if you cannot say something in 10 minutes it is not worth saying- is not not enough time to put some points in this country as a national federal politician because some statements cannot be put eloquently in 10 minutes or less.
How do you speak, Madam Speaker, about a Meech Lake constitutional package, for instance, in less than 10 minutes? How do you speak about a Persian Gulf crisis in less than 10 minutes? How do you describe how one feels when one looks at the Kurds, in less than 10 minutes? Sure, we can discuss some aspect for five minutes and that is plenty of time. But on many other issues, ten minutes does not do justice to the substance of the day. And who is to decide which issue deserves five minutes and which deserves unlimited discussion in this beautiful chamber we ought to protect, in every sense of the word?
Therefore, on some of those changes, I am opposed, because, if you look at this chamber, it is a magnificent chamber. I remember the very first time I came here as a visitor, in early 1980. Seeing the chamber was very different from viewing it from a distance or reading about it in the newspaper. It reminded me of the first time I went to Maple Leaf Gardens. You can watch a hockey game, as many Canadians are doing this evening, and you can say it is a great game. Then you go into Maple Leaf Gardens and there is an ambiance, there are lights, and there are pictures on the wall. It is history in action and it gives you a different sense.
That was the same feeling I had when I came up and sat in the visitor's gallery and looked at the lights, the wood carvings, and the history that embodies this place. It is truly a remarkable place, that is the envy of the world, that we sometimes take for granted, that sometimes does not work, in which we sometimes do not listen to each other on enough occasions, that sometimes becomes too partisan, yes, but that has also lost a bit of relevance over the last few years, that has sensed a loss of power in the last few years, and that is concentrated more in the executive of a government.
If we are to give a sense of better purpose to this magnificent place and if we are to give a greater sense of
Government Orders
purpose to individual Members of Parliament, who have been elected by a large number of Canadians, who have their franchise to make important decisions on their behalf, then we cannot contemplate some of the changes being proposed to us in these rule changes we are debating.
If we want Parliament to be more responsive, if we want it to be more relevant, and if we want to give the opposition a chance to hold the power and the government in check, then we have to approach it in a very different sense from that by which this government is approaching it. Unfortunately, I get the sense that this is a government that does not have the intention of spending too much time in this place.
But that view is short lived. This government has come and this government will go. This opposition will also change. You and I will one day hopefully be looking on a very different parliament and we have to look at a parliament in its long-term context. This Parliament does not belong to this government, this opposition, or this Speaker. We are simply custodians for a four- to five-year period. What we are doing this week is possibly changing the way this place operates for years to come.
With that sense in mind, we ought to move in the right direction and with dignity. We ought to restore some of the respect and dignity of this place and of the members who occupy it, which have so regrettably been lost and eroded in the last number of years.

Madam Speaker, I want to thank you for the opportunity to participate in this debate.
I am hoping this evening to talk about a couple of points that are not necessarily contained in this package but might be, because when we examine the rules and rule changes we can consider what changes we are making, but doing so also gives us an opportunity to talk about some changes that we might wish to make in the future.
Some members have talked about some of these rule changes, both positively and negatively. Most have dwelt on the amount of time Parliament may or may not be sitting, either more or less, or in a different way. Frankly, I do not really believe that aspect is particularly relevant. I do not mean that as a negative comment toward the people who have spoken, but it seems to me that the changes being proposed here are not particularly revolu-

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
tionaiy and will not change the nature of how we operate in any substantial way. That is why I would like to suggest a couple of changes a little further along that might change things substantially.
Part of the problem, I believe, is that there is a substantial gap between what the public believes we do here and what goes on. One of those gaps, if you like, has been brought closer to the forefront in recent times under the Spicer commission and other forums in which the public has increasingly been saying that they believe there should be more free votes in Parliament, less ties to party lines, and less control by the party or the leaders of parties.
That is probably an interesting point and a good one, but, in part, it reflects the fact that most Canadians do not understand exactly what Parliament does and what kinds of matters it deals with. That is not to say anything negative about them, because frankly, until I got here, neither did I. But the issue is not free votes. In my opinion, virtually every vote we have had in the time I have been here has been free. I know that the votes usually break down along party lines, but I think we have to explore how that happens.
When I examine the last two years of Parliament, in this session, I see that we have introduced approximately 100 bills. I looked through those bills and determined that of those bills, only 14 had what I would call substantive votes.
I want to explain that a bit. We have a lot of votes around this place which involve such things as voting when to adjourn or not to adjourn, whether someone can speak or not speak, whether or not to move to Orders of the Day. If we examine the votes which occur on substantive issues, and even though in some cases there may be several votes involving the same bill or issue, we call that one vote, because obviously it is essentially consistent. We may have moved to Orders of the Day and done a number of other things to trigger the vote, so several votes may be involved. But we can narrow it down to how many issues Parliament divides on which are substantive. Of the 100 bills, about 85 per cent of them passed through this House on division or on a voice vote. In other words, no recorded vote was demanded. It was supported by the House.
Only about a dozen bills, in actual fact, required a formal division by the House. In some cases more than
one division is taken, but as I say we will look at them one issue at a time.
Of those 12 or 14 bills, four or five were divisions triggered by something else. On the Broadcasting Act, Bill C-40, there was substantial support in the House but because cutbacks had been announced to the CBC the day before, there was a protest vote, so to speak, which triggered the formal vote.
On the borrowing authority, by and large no one in this House plans to vote down the borrowing authority. But sometimes it can be used to send a message to the government or to extract other things.
If we really narrow it down to this session of Parliament, of the 100 bills, in my opinion, we have had only four or five substantive votes. One, everybody would realize was on the GST, and we may have voted several times involving that issue but really there was only one issue involved. There was another vote involving some income tax amendments, including what we call colloquially the clawback. There was Bill C-21, amendments to the unemployment insurance, and there was the privatization of Petro-Canada and perhaps one or two others.
What I am saying is that on virtually every issue on which there was a substantive vote, where people voted because they were voting in terms of the issue, the vote did break down on party lines. That is relatively natural, because if we are talking about privatizing Petro-Cana-da, one can presume that most members of the Conservative Party would be in favour of that, most members of the New Democratic Party would not, and so it is only natural that it would break down along party lines.
If every vote was formally and officially a free vote, the question is would there be any difference. I suggest that, no, there would not. The reason is that for a whole bunch of issues out there which the public is concerned about, no vote is ever held-or if it is, no vote is ever held that would have any effect on the issue.
Consider three or four of the controversial issues over the last five or six years that I have been involved in while I have been here in Parliament. For example, consider the CF-18 contract, when Petro-Canada purchased Gulf or the issue of Sikhs and turbans and whether or not RCMP members would be allowed to wear turbans. None of those things were decided by a vote of Parliament, they were all decided by executive

decision, by decisions of cabinet ministers involved or by the cabinet as a whole. None of those issues which the public was interested in and which were important to them were decided by a vote.
I am suggesting that it is not a matter of free votes or not free votes, it is the matter of what comes to a vote in this House. That is determined, by and large, by the executive, by the government, the cabinet. In actual fact very few votes are held on substantive issues that are not going to break down on party lines or are not going to pass through the House without a declared vote.
This whole issue of allowing more free votes of freeing members from party lines to support their constituents, is a bit of a red herring.
The question becomes, what can we do about it? One of the things we can do is try to educate the public as to how this place works, but after about 125 years that this Parliament has been in existence I am not sure that anything is going to really change in the future.
One of the other things we might do is allow more issues to be voted on. This could be done by allowing individual items coming from members of Parliament to be voted on.
We have had various changes in Private Members' Business since I have been here. However, because of the system we now have, none of these changes are likely to bring substantive issues to the table. Among other things, first of all, there is the lottery system, which means our name has to be drawn to have our item even selected. Then, there is another system that decides whether that item is going to come to a vote.
I would like to suggest that one of the things we might do is consider allowing bills to be introduced at committee stage.
One of the complaints that has been made is that there are some restrictions in terms of allocated times for certain stages of the bills. I suggest that we might want to consider abolishing second reading altogether. Perhaps we could restrict it to an introduction and response on the bill by each party. Automatically the bill could be sent to committee to be studied.
Government Orders
At that time, we could gather the information and examine it carefully. When it comes back to the House, we could have the substantive debate. Part of the problem now is that in making a commitment or virtually deciding in advance of any study how people are going to line up on a particular bill or issue, we pre-determine how they are going to react when we get to committee. In my view, it prejudices the kind of debate or examination that might take place. We could avoid that by sending bills to committee automatically after only minimal discussion.
I have been involved in the changes made in the committee system. Some of them have been good. I have been on one of the committees which has worked as well as any of the committees of the House; that is, the finance committee. The reason it has worked well is that members have chosen to take an independent view from the government from time to time. That has been supported by all members, including the opposition members.
What has not happened in our committee or in other committees is that opposition members have not taken independent views from their party's position. As a result of that, the system has not been very balanced. That is not an argument against the parties or the individuals, it is because they have no real vested interest in doing so.
One of the reasons for that is because the position of their party has already been made known at the second reading vote. It seems to me that if we would introduce bills and have them referred to committee, they could be considered in a serious way in committee. Then they could be sent to the House.
In making that examination, we would not necessarily have the committed points of view and partisanship that goes along with it. I recognize that I have not thought out all the ramifications and how this might work, but I do acknowledge that I have been looking essentially at the United States system where by and large bills are introduced at committee stage. Once bills pass that hurdle, they then get considered by the House as a whole. It seems to me that if we were to allow both private members and the government to introduce bills, then they would have to compete for the attention and support of committee members. Those members would

then decide those things that needed to be moved further along.
In a parliamentary system, a government-the cabinet and the executive-will have to move those things and decide support. That would have to be preserved. It is preserved right now. The House of Commons and the cabinet through the House can invoke closure, if you like, on a bill at committee stage and have it brought back to the House.
They have the ability even in our current system to set the priorities. What I would like to suggest is that rather than having a system of Private Members' Business where first the bills have to be drawn and then decided by a committee of Parliament which of them have priority and which get voted, in advance of that stage, bills would have to come through the committee involved. If I decided that I had a bill I wanted to present that involved labour, for example, I would have to convince the House of Commons committee on labour, employment and immigration, I believe it is called now-we change the names around here so often I have trouble keeping track-that my bill was worthy of support. In terms of the priority of that committee and the agenda and the other things it had to do, my bill would have to compete for their attention. It would consider my bill. It might examine it; hear witnesses and decide that it could move forward. Only after that would it then compete for House of Commons time, either in a separately allocated period of time within the private members' period that we now have, or perhaps in conjunction with other bills and other time in what we currently call Government Orders.
I think this would be helpful because it would allow committees to consider matters right from the very beginning and would allow committees to decide some of their own priorities, leaving the government the ability to bring forward those items that it decided was a priority.
The other thing it would allow is items to come before committees and, perhaps, the House to be voted on by people who are really interested in it. As I tried to point out in my earlier remarks, the issue is not free votes. If every vote was officially and formally a free vote, in the past two years, chances are virtually no votes would have been different. Mine would not have been. I can think of one bill in six years as a member of Parliament that I
might have opposed and voted differently from my party and the leadership.
As I have said, the reason for that is these items never get presented. If a bill is introduced by a minister and warning signals are picked up by the House leader, because that is the House leader's job, to know that this particular bill might not gamer the support of virtually all members of the government, that bill simply sits on the Order Paper.
The public, of course, never sees government members voting against government bills. That is because the government does not bring a bill to be voted if there might be substantial opposition to it or danger of losing it. It then becomes the responsibility of the minister responsible for the bill to work out whatever problems there are so that at least all the government members, if not the opposition members, are satisfied.
I do not think that the number of days and hours that we sit here, more or less, is important. By changing those and changing how we allocate them to the calendar might make it more convenient for members, including me, and I am all for that. I do not think it is going to make a substantial change to the way this House does business or to the way the public perceives us. What will make a change is if we decide to have issues aired and perhaps voted that the public thinks are important.
As I said earlier, I do not think that most debates really contribute all that much to whether a bill is advanced or not. Again, in my six years as a member of Parliament, I can probably count on one hand the number of debates that were true debates and actually affected the thinking of members. The opposition parties want to keep the debate going and the government wants to respond in kind, so we present speeches, not for making arguments or changing people's minds, but to fill up the available time. We all do that and we are all guilty, including myself.
We would be far better off spending less time on time filling and more time on substantive debate on issues that people are truly interested in. In fact, that might be part of overcoming what I call the gap between the current attitude of the public that Parliament does not respond to the things they are interested in. They also believe that we are always voting for and following either our parties or our leadership or what we are told by the Prime Minister or the leader or whoever it happens to be. It is not how much time we spend in debate, or even
