Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have the opportunity to speak on the proposed changes to the Standing Orders. I think that these changes are really very severe. Some have called them Draconian distortions of the parliamentary and democratic process here in the Chamber.
As has been presented many times this evening, the changes that have been presented-and there are man-y-by the government through the House leader are changes that are essentially going to muzzle Parliament. If the changes are brought to fruition, Parliament will essentially cease to be accountable to the Canadian people, at least as much as it is at this point. There is some concern across Canada that we are already not accountable enough.
I can see that these changes would not be the reformation of Parliament but, in fact, the deformation of Parliament. The Prime Minister's assertion that the aim of these proposed changes will be to allow the members to be more accountable and more available to their ridings really is the greatest hypocrisy. While members may, with these changes, be able to spend more time in their ridings, I think it will be a moot point since the government will not be as accountable to the concerns brought up by the people in the ridings when they talk with their member of Parliament. I will get into that in just a little while.
If the aim of the government is really to increase accountability and the democratic process, I suggest we are going about it in the wrong way. What it is going to do is increase the distrust and the anger that is already out across Canada, the anger that Canadians feel in regard to their lack of access to Canada's Parliament. If these changes are brought to bear, which undoubtedly they will because we are speaking on closure debate tonight, this government and particularly this House leader is going to become known as the Grinch who stole democracy.
Government Orders
The first argument in support of my concern is that the changes that the government is proposing reduces the actual sitting time of this House by some 40 days, or if we want to do it on a percentage basis, by some 25 per cent. The committees, and this has been discussed many times tonight, as they are currently structured, will certainly not meet as often. I want to point out that today was the first day in literally months when the standing committee on communications of which I am a member met, even though there have been many veiy important and critical issues that have happened in the whole area of communications and broadcasting. Thke, for example, the situation with the CBC. Canadians right across this country have rallied against the CBC cuts and have spoken strongly about their concerns. They faced the shock of these cuts. Yet this committee has failed to meet on these very important changes that are being proposed to the CBC. If these changes are brought forward through the changes in the House Standing Orders, these committees will have even less opportunity to meet.
Under the old rules, committees meet infrequently enough. Some of them are much more active than others. Some of them are essentially completely inactive. The argument I am trying to make is that under these proposed new changes, these committees would meet even less often and would also be restricted in who could actually address the committee. The government is restricting it to what it calls those witnesses that it wants to call forward would be witnesses who would have some technical expertise.
No longer would it seem that community advocacy groups or individuals who are concerned about proposed legislative changes would have access to the standing committees as they do now. Those committees would be restricted to calling forth witnesses who would be of witnesses of technical expertise.
I think that is a very serious restriction on the public's right to voice their concerns, their opinions on the legislation that is before us, on the legislation that is being imposed by the government. Lord knows that with the technological changes facing our society, with the vast amount of legislation that is before the House, legislation which in some cases is extremely technical,

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
and the changes very profound indeed, one has to rely upon those witnesses, both expert and lay person, who want to come forth to the committee to give their concerns, to raise their objections to the changes. I submit that with the restrictions on the committee structure, this is not going to be able to take place.
I want to reflect back to when I served for a couple of years as the member of the legislative assembly for the North Okanagan back in 1984 to 1986. During the two years that I was provincial MLA, with the government of the day under Premier Bill Bennett, the committee structure there did not work at all. I can recall being very excited about being nominated to the select standing committee on environmental issues and was very excited with the opportunities that that presented. I was literally shocked to find that the committee met only once over the two years I was there and that was to basically select a chairperson and a secretary and subsequent to that did not meet at all. As a result, there was virtually no opportunity to have a decent review of the legislation before us.
That was a very difficult situation. I suggest there was a lot of poor legislation that came through during those years simply because the public did not have access to a procedure of appeal through the committee structure to allow them to present their concerns about some of the legislation that was coming through.
I want to say that I think we are in danger through the changes that are being presented in these changes to the Standing Orders of approaching that kind of very unacceptable situation here in our federal institution.
Another argument I want to present is that I think that the changes are being proposed are an attempt by this government to seal the lips of the opposition. There is going to be a reduction in the number of opposition days, the number of days that opposition parties have to propose their topic for the agenda of the day, for their motion to be debated.
There is going to be a reduction in those days where the opposition has its own day in court, so to speak. There is going to be a reduction in the number of days of debate on the throne speech and on the budget.
The end result is really veiy convenient, if you look at it from the government side, I guess, a very convenient muzzling of the opposition voice in terms of the democratic process. Opposition and government members may have more time to go to their ridings, find out what their constituents think and how they are feeling. We are actually reducing the ability of the forum where those views could be aired. We are actually reducing the effectiveness of the parliamentary forum with the changes that are proposed.
I have heard a lot of comments made previously by one of the government members who resides in British Columbia about how difficult it is to get back and forth to the west coast. I certainly agree with him, as a member also from British Columbia. I am from the interior of British Columbia. My riding is in the central southern part of the province, the Okanagan-Shuswap.
It is indeed a lengthy trip back and forth between the Kelowna airport, either through Vancouver and Calgary, and then on through Toronto, or directly to Ottawa. I figured it out that on an average trip, depending on the connections, it takes B.C. members, particularly if they are having to make the jog up into the interior of the province, between nine and eleven hours to get doorstep to doorstep. There is no question that with the length of travel, some of us travel more often in a month than some of the airline pilots log. There is no hiding the fact that it is difficult indeed for most members, particularly the members from the western provinces.
As well, you are dealing with three-hour time zone changes which are pretty disruptive to the old biological time clock. I would be the first to admit that. But even with the difficulties that are imposed on the westernmost representatives in this federal Parliament, I would still submit that it is a mistake for these changes to come through which reduce the parliamentary voice of opposition members in this institution through the reduction of the hours, only to give us more time back in our ridings.
I try to split my time up each month and take a week out, if I can, when I do not have duty days here in Parliament, and spend that week-and I must submit, probably most weekends also-back in the riding. There is no question, there is a lot of travel.

I think if you want to be an effective representative, despite whether your riding might be an hour away in Montreal, or nine or eleven hours away up in B.C. or the Yukon, if you do want to be an effective representative of your constituency, you can do that under the current parliamentary structure. You can continue to be effective representatives and yet still have the kind of parliamentary forum that we need in order to have an effective debate of the issues, and in order to have an effective opposition.
If you do not have an effective opposition, you have the next thing to dictatorship in this country. I think it is extremely important that the opposition voice not be muzzled by the kinds of changes that are being proposed in these changes to the parliamentary rules.
The other argument I want to submit is with respect to the reduction of speaking time. It is proposed to reduce speaking time down from 20 minutes to 10 minutes with respect to members speaking on legislation before the House.
I go back to the point I made before. Often we are dealing with legislation in this House that is extremely difficult, extremely complex, very technical. I submit that Bill C-40, the Broadcast Act, when it came through had a lot of intricate detail in that legislation. There is simply no way that a person can stand up and in 10 minutes give a detailed and thoughtful explanation as to why he or she may support or oppose the legislation, to give the details of that information and fully explain the reasons for either supporting or opposing the legislation. Ten minutes is simply not enough. I often think 20 minutes is not enough. We need more time to speak. But the rules that are being proposed take us to a reduced time allocation, and I think that is a serious mistake.
Last, the fifth point, and I think probably the most insidious changes that these changes to the rules suggest, is the government's ability to override unanimous consent. Through this, the government is trying to override a very fundamental principle of Parliament that essentially one person can make a difference.
I want to explain myself on that. I do not think one person should be able to take the decision away from the majority. That is not what I am suggesting. Regardless of whether it is a strong majority government or a minority government, one person, as a public representative, a federal representative in this Parliament, should be able
Government Orders
to force the government to play by the rules, play by the book and use the democratic process.
The greatest irony is that by using closure, this government will in fact be able to impose those kinds of changes which muzzle the voice of the opposition, closure that has been used during the last three years no fewer than 13 times. It does not sound like a lot, 13, but when you look at it in terms of the historical precedence in Parliament, over the last two or three years the use of closure 13 times is more than half of all the times that closure was used in the House during the previous 75 years of government. In the last three years, we have used closure far more than during those previous times.
I think the people across the country are beginning to look upon the Canadian political system with a certain amount of disdain. I do not think that these changes are in the best interest of Canadians. They are certainly going to harden that feeling against Canada's parliamentary system.
When we go back and look at the history of this last Parliament, people have seen the government using closure on the free trade debate and the imposition of free trade despite the fact the country did not want it. Closure was used on the GST debate. Now, in addition to using that process of closure, these rule changes essentially allow the government to cloak its actions in secrecy; 40 fewer Question Periods, fewer opposition days, and the many other changes that are being mentioned.
I think the changes, in short, are going to turn this parliamentary system into kind of a legislative sausage factory, if you like, a kind of a legislative assembly line where really there are no inspections, no taste tests and there is no ability of the opposition to slow down or to stop dead in its tracks poor legislation or to provide the opportunity in order to make that legislation, if it is supported, better.
In concluding, forcing these kinds of changes that are proposed and proclaiming that it is so, that all members of Parliament can participate more in their riding activities, I think is ludicrous and is really hiding the fact. The fact of the matter is that the changes are being brought to bear because this government does not want to take the kind of heat that it has been taking and, quite frankly, it should be taking in bringing through the

Mr. Speaker, I would like to just enter the debate in a very brief way because I think everyone should have an opportunity to participate in what I consider to be a very historical debate in this House of Commons.
I submit that the whole world is in a change. We see the world changing, not only going from one-party systems in the East Bloc but hopefully to a multi-party system where there is a democracy as the Canadian people have known it for some 125 years. They would like to have that opportunity.
Let me tell you, I am not going to speak for more than five minutes because I do not need 20 minutes to say what I think is important in terms of how this place operates. I have a lot of respect for the last speaker, the hon. member for Okanagan-Shuswap. His party would like to form the government next time. If it does form the government the next time, he probably would be happy as can be with such a move as has taken place in this House.
I submit that the change this government is asking for, although I respect that it is not perfect, I think it is going to take us out of the 18th century. I follow the U.S. congressional and senatorial system on television through C-Span, through the communication devices today. With all respect to the systems that we have in place here and in England, I do not see that adversarial activity that I see in this House of Commons. There seems to be a lot of respect for each representative, a great deal more respect than we show each other in this House.
I ask myself why are they not using every kind of motion and different methods of changing legislation as we do rather than just good honest debate. That is what we should be doing. Colleagues across the way, you and I should be debating. We should not take the time for petitions. In my view, you should send the petitions up to the desk-you don't have to take time to announce them-and stand in your place and debate the legislation that is put forward.
Obviously, your position will be different. But I do not believe that we have to get at each other's ideas in the
adversarial way such as I have experienced in the last six years.
We do not have to talk for 20 minutes, with all due respect, to put a point across. The committees should sit and debate positions in a manner that is not adversarial. I have not experienced that. I wonder why.
Even in this Chamber I would like to see changes. I would like to see changes to your dress, Sir. Put an ordinary suit on, like the Speaker in the U.S. Congress. That is not going to show any less respect for our institution. We do not have to dress people up in a different way. In my view, we could even go further, and I would have no difficulty with that.
But let me tell you something as I see it. I have not sat in opposition. Heaven knows, that likely could happen some day. I am not advocating that, but should the day come, because I may disagree with a piece of legislation that has been proposed by the government, I would not see myself as trying to present petitions all day to stall the debate on that legislation, or presenting dilatory motions to stop the debate on the legislation because I disagree with it. Should not that time be spent on debate?
I hear from across the way they should storm the Chair. Yes, I understand that the Tory in the past in opposition have stormed the Chair. That is nonsense. I do not agree with that. I would not be a part of such an action.
That is what has happened over the years, I believe, to the deterioration of our House of Commons, a place that is so important. We have lost respect for different people in this Chamber from time to time because of something they said. I don't think that action has been very helpful.
I must submit, as a sitting member of the government side, that I have seen wasted hours of debate in this House, wasted hours of debate by playing silly games. Maybe my five minutes is up, but my point is, with all due respect, that we have wasted hours and hours and hours of debate in this House of Commons by playing games.
Now, now, you are falling into the role again, with all due respect. We have wasted hours of debate because of a procedural wrangle.

Those 20-some hours that I believe the change adds up to would probably not have been lost to anyone. Who knows who the opposition is going to be next time? I am not conceding defeat but I am saying that the people opposite in this House today obviously hope that they are going to govern after the next election. That is their goal, there is no doubt about it. But, surely to goodness, when they are there some day-heaven forbid, some may say-we do not want to spend this time on silliness.
The House of Commons in England. I have not been there as often as some in this Chamber. In the United States Congress and Senate, there are not many times when people are able to speak for 20 minutes, because there are many more of them than there are of us. They may get to speak for five minutes and will then yield three minutes to someone else to bring their point of view across to the floor.
I am just wondering if we are not so hung up on this institution and its historical way that we should not think of changing it and making it more effective. Although this is not a perfect package and there is probably more change to come as years go by, I believe it is moving in the right direction. I think members opposite will concede that we are not still going to run the House of Commons as we did 20 or 50 years ago. Changes are taking place.
This is a vast nation to represent and I do not think anybody is upset about the time he or she has to spend in this place. But I like honest, fair debate and when the day is done the vote is taken and we go on to another issue. That is something I have lacked, but I have nothing but respect for our members opposite. I even disagree sometimes with members on our side of the House and I think that is healthy. I do not think that is totally antiquated anymore; that is our democracy and our freedom.
I believe we have moved away a little from operating this House and have created it as too adversarial. I hope the change that does come forward works more effectively for all sides of the House, albeit there may be less time in hours, but in the end I do believe in the representation we have in this House and the honour we should attribute to one another, not in the adversarial approach. Make your point, let us get on with it and take a vote on it. That is the way I see it and I believe I will support this.

Mr. Speaker, I have to commend the member for Portage- Interlake. There are some things he and I agree on. I think we have the same taste in what we do not like, such as so-called modem art, when you see something that looks like the side of a bam, where they ran out of one pail of paint and had to dive into another. He and I agree on that. We agree on what we should be doing with steaks. I would rather see a vibrant living picture or piece of art and I am sure you would, too; something that would reflect nature and the delicate hand of mother nature.
But I do have to say that I disagree with him saying that he would rather have something like the American congressional or Senate system, where the speaker wears a suit, the same as everyone else.
Mr. Speaker, you and your Chair are the symbol of the tradition of this House, a tradition that instils the tradition of a democratic parliamentary system, which respects the Chair and the Speaker, who is elected by the members of this House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, we are all commoners and are elected by commoners to represent them in this House and I would not want that changed. I want to state the respect in which I hold you, Mr. Speaker, the other Deputy Speakers, and the Speaker himself.
One of the things I am very concerned about is that, as I look back at the record of this government and at the number of times they have used closure, going back to 1986-1987, they have used it 35 times. Yet the member from Portage-Interlake said that every member should have a chance to speak.
When I look at the record of this House and, again, at the number of times closure has been applied by this government, the successes of the legislation, the effectiveness of the legislation, the impact of the legislation on the economy and society, and at how this government has used the application of closure, I realize that this government is becoming more and more one that governs by corporate decision and that responds more to big business than to the wishes of the people who elected its members.
The government is going to use its majority here tonight, as we near the end of this session, to bring about changes that will cut the sitting days of this House and will deprive the members of this House of an opportunity

Government Orders
to fully represent the wishes and needs of their constituents.
As I reflect on this package of real changes and on the cut in the number of sitting days involved, and as I look back on the last two and a half years and on the fact that closure has been consistently used by this government rather than allowing each member to speak and allowing full debate, I could not help but think back to about 35 years ago next month. I want to quote from Hansard of that time:
The first duty of Parliament is to remain a Parliament, not to become a subservient and ornamental body.
Parliament has a right that is certainly paramount to the convenience of the Prime Minister and has the right to live. It also has the duty to defend itself and to not allow anybody to invade its rights and privileges. It is the will of Parliament, not of the government, that is the will of the nation.
When the Prime Minister says he speaks for the whole country he is mistaking the echoes of his own words for the voice of the Canadian people. Parliament is and must remain the authorized exponent of public opinion and public will. The sovereignty of the people is delegated to the Parliament, not to the executive.
When I say Parliament, I mean the minority as well as the majority in Parliament. However, I do make an appeal to the Prime Minister that this Parliament and this institution should be a temple of freedom, not a place where frustration becomes a means whereby rights are swept aside and where rules are misinterpreted in order to achieve a temporary advantage.
Those words accurately reflect what we are seeing here today and were uttered by the late Rt. Hon. John Diefenbaker, who became Prime Minister. After a statement such as that, I wonder what he would say if he was here today and listened to this debate and saw the further erosion of the role of the members of this institution.
Closure was applied on three agriculture bills in second reading. First of all, we had the bill on plant breeders' rights. Let me tell you, the jury is still out on that one. The opposition insisted there were far too many years of protection and of the continued corporate acquisitions that are taking place in society today, and of the takeovers. We may well rue the day when we provided the legislative foundation for a few veiy powerful corporate structures to control the world's food chain.
Then, of course, the government applied closure to the Advance Payments of Crops Act and the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act. We tried to tell the
government they were wrong and numerous witnesses in committee supported us in the Official Opposition, but rather than allow the adequate debate of second reading and, even worse, rather than listen to what we in the Official Opposition had to say, this government bulldozed ahead with their majority of trained seals, who actually believed their minister rather us on this side, who actually had the base of experience and knowledge of the industry.
If the members had listened to us in the Official Opposition they would not have suffered the embarrassment of having to reinstate those interest-free loans. That must have been a terrible embarrassment to them because they had to turn around and eat humble pie last fall due to the huge crop and the low prices of grain in Canada.
Not only was the government proven wrong and embarrassed, but their credibility has fallen to even further lows. Only experienced farmers can tell them what is going to happen, but perhaps it was fate itself that intervened and their embarrassment is certainly justified because of their unwarranted application of closure before all members on this side of the House had the opportunity to speak.
As if closure on the Advance Payments of Crops Act was not enough, the government applied closure again on Bill C-48, the Crop Insurance Act, when it came before this House. We again opposed it and they again invoked closure at second reading and again in committee. The witnesses all asked that the government not proceed with the legislation. Of course, that bill has now been replaced by the GRIP legislation or the safety net legislation.
That legislation has been flaunted as the greatest thing since sliced bread, but when I compare that program to the programs of the farmers in the country to the south of us I believe it will be found lacking. A safety net is slung just a little bit above the ground. It may cushion the landing somewhat, but it will not enable the farmers to survive continuing years of low prices. This is just another example of this government not listening to the Official Opposition or to the witnesses in committee.
We have another example: Bill C-26, the At and East legislation that eliminated the rail subsidy for grain being

transported by rail into Atlantic Canada during the winter months when the St. Lawrence Seaway is closed.
Those people needed grain down there over the winter and they did not have storage in which to hold it all. This legislation was originally put in place to enable the railways to supply that grain in order to keep the Atlantic industry alive, their flour mills going, and their elevators in use.
We opposed that legislation at second reading, in committee, and at report stage. Do you know, I believe they finally realized when we reached report stage what a blunder would have resulted from this legislation. Not only were elevators and flour mills in Atlantic Canada faced with closing, but a huge loss of jobs and a traditional market for grain from western Canada would now be filled with grain from another country. What a blunder.
In fact, the elevators in the minister's own riding in Georgian Bay were demolished because of this ill-conceived legislation. The only good thing I can say about it is that the government apparently must have realized its blunder because it never brought that bill forward from Report stage for passage on third reading. I suspect the government is simply trying to avoid further embarrassment over the error of its ways. The damage was done and those elevators were demolished and it is doubtful whether they will ever be rebuilt.
Surely, if this government had listened to the opposition and had paid attention to our concerns instead of marching to the tune of the corporate elite and their idols to the south, it would not have approved the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement in its present form. The Conservatives would not be as embarrassed as they are now over the pork ruling that Carla Hills has rejected. They would have had a fairer agreement; one that would absolutely forbid the use of subsidies to steal our grain markets with export enhancement subsidies. Now they are so embarrassed that they have not been able to screw up enough courage to demand consultation, as provided for in the Free Trade Agreement, or to demand compensation for our grain producers, as provided for in that agreement, which they negotiated.
We have seen these things happen, as I have outlined here tonight. One would think that, rather than cut back on the number of sitting days, the government would
Government Orders
have wanted to increase them in order to give the opposition more time to point out the blunders and mistakes in the legislation it has brought forward and to then amend that legislation, in keeping with the advice of the witnesses in committee and with the amendments proposed by the Official Opposition.
I am alarmed about the erosion of the role of the members of this House and of the democratic system of government that has served this nation so well since Confederation. With the problems facing this nation today, whether national unity, the economy, the millions of people who are out of work in this country, the state of affairs across rural Canada, the closing-down of our post offices, or the boarding-up of businesses in the small towns and villages across this nation, surely it is time this government should not be cutting back on the time permitted for Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition. Rather, we should be calling Parliament more often and it should be sitting more often to make sure the needs and aspirations of the people of this nation are adhered to.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is close to 10 p.m. on this Thursday, April 11. Canadian unity is in a state of crisis, our citizens are losing their jobs, agriculture is in serious difficulty, there is a 16.6 per cent unemployment rate in my riding, and the government has decided that the hottest topic for us to talk about is whether we should change our rules, to give ourselves more time off.
I wonder if the Canadians who are watching this debate tonight or who will read Hansard during the next few days will be impressed by the choice of subject of today's debate; a choice made, of course, by the government across the way.
As you and I know, Mr. Speaker, under our rules, the government brings forward the legislation we deal with. The House collectively decides how it disposes of the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, tonight we are talking abaut amending the Standing Orders in this difficult period when we could be talking about something else. Have you noticed, that when the House sits, when Parliament is debating hot issues, important issues of the day, it is rarely advantageous to the government? This is not peculiar to the period we are now in. I think that historically, when Parliament sits, having the House and its members

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
question the government and hold it accountable certainly does not always make them popular for doing so.

I have in hand a public opinion poll dated March 21, 1991, which speaks of the level of popularity of the various political parties. Without making a diatribe about all of them, suffice it to say that, according to that particular poll, the present government had a popularity rating of some 16 per cent according to the Gallup organization.
It is no coincidence that the people are upset with governments that choose, in difficult times such as the one we are living in, to debate this particular issue instead of all the other issues that could be on the public agenda.
I have listened with attention to the member for Selkirk-Interlake, whom, of course, I respect very much. The member for Selkirk-Interlake always has a grass-roots approach to stating matters and I agree with many things he says. Tonight, though, I will have to part with some of his statements, such as when he remarked how we should modernize our so-called institution by removing some of the traditions we have. I will use the Speaker's attire as one and perhaps the Clerks attire, the Mace, and those other objects of tradition that we have.
They are not only part of a fetish we have for conserving old museum-like ideas, but represent in our parliamentary system 1,000 years of parliamentary democracy. Every one of those objects is a part of those traditions and every time we see those objects we remind ourselves of those years during which people fought to achieve the freedom we have.
That Mace on the table represents an ancient object that was not a decoration with which to represent authority, but something with which people would arm themselves. We all know there was also a time when that object was necessary for the physical protection of the institution.
Today, that object is still necessary, not because we want to club a member over the head with it, although I suppose that, from time to time, that temptation might arise on the part of some, but to remind ourselves of the fact that the Mace stands for those years when people fought to give us the freedom we now have.
The role of the opposition and of Parliament in this type of democratic institution is to debate. It is not a luxury to debate the important issues of our country. This is not the pure legislative chamber they have in certain democracies. I will use the example of the United States. It is partly that, of course, but it is also a place where we can raise the aspirations, the feelings and express the grievances of those who sent us here.
You might recall, and I say this to all colleagues in the House, a couple of years ago when Patrick Watson produced the television series entitled, I believe, The Struggle for Democracy. I watched that series very closely. In one episode they dealt with the October crisis of 1970. I watched attentively the interpretation of that particular episode.
It was interesting to note that Mr. Watson, when presenting this issue, was telling us that in 1970 the democratic rights of people were removed by the invocation of the War Measures Act, that this particular action was decided by the government and adopted, according to him, very quickly by the House of Commons with little debate.
I will not get into the issue as to whether or not the action was appropriate at that time. I happened to think that it was, but that is a subject we can debate at some other time. That is not the issue I am bringing to your attention. Mr. Watson was basically transmitting the message that the opposition and Parliament as a whole had not questioned the government properly, had not held the government to account, had not opposed in such a way as to make the government justify what it was doing. For that, according to him, the opposition was to blame, not the government, because it had failed in its duty to question. That is our job, to question the government.
Similarly, Mr. Watson made the same criticism of the press. They had not held the government to account as it is necessary to preserve democracy. It is not a foreign concept, it is the same in our courts. I am not a lawyer, but we watch how our courts operate, with both sides producing the most eloquent argument that they can for the position they strongly believe in.

Some people better than others.
April 11, 1991

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Some people better than others, says the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Quite true, but the point is that the adversarial system in Parliament and in the courts has not exactly been wrong. As a matter of fact, I would like to think that it has been good. It has been good because we have been able, I, as an opposition member, and I speak with lots of experience because I have not sat on the government side yet-hopefully that will change soon-and other members as government members saying what they believe in. Ultimately the public reacts to our debates, the people listen to what we have to say, the media report what we have to say, editorials are formed, people's thoughts are gathered and eventually the process changes when it is not sufficiently appropriate to meet the expectations of people, or at least generally it does.
It is not perfect and, yes, there are days in which time goes by here and there is delay. I have seen a lot of that. I have seen that as an employee of this building, I have seen that as a member of this Parliament and I have seen that in my previous role as a member of a provincial legislature. But all of that process is not useless. The process is used to express the wishes and the aspirations of those who sent us here.
Governments have been known to change their minds about policies in the past. The opposition, and even government backbenchers, have raised important issues in this House repeatedly. Because people in the media have reported on those debates repeatedly, and because constituents have phoned their members of Parliament to express their opinion on what they heard, what had been said in the House and what had been reported in the media repeatedly, ultimately that has served us well.
It is a delicate balance that we have. I recognize that. Others in the past have recognized that. The rules of this House were changed some years ago, after the report of the Lefebvre committee, now Senator Lefebvre, who was a great member of this House. Senator Lefebvre chaired this committee which reported on proposed rule changes. The House decided to adopt the rules. The rules had been adopted unanimously at committee and the House decided to adopt them. They did not decide to adopt some and reject others, but they adopted the report.
Government Orders
In the case of the McGrath rules, again a very distinguished member-a different political party, but nevertheless a man I have a lot of respect for-presided over a committee in the mid-1980s and again, we looked at what had been proposed and agreed to unanimously by the committee. But this time the government set off on a dangerous precedent.

And I said so then in the House, Mr. Speaker. The government chose parts of the McGrath Report to adopt and of course left out others. Fine. I said then, Mr. Speaker, that the government today chooses parts of a report. The precedent is there. From now on, whole reports will no longer be adopted. The government will change the rules as it sees fit, because the door had been opened to it that day and today is the second step. Today, we see a whole series of changes with which the opposition members of Parliament do not agree.

Those rules, unbalanced as they are, give advantage to the government, make the government less accountable. There are fewer Question Periods in which this government can justify to the people of Canada what it does and does not do for them. If that process makes a few bills pass more quickly, well, I suppose there will be two or three people, perhaps, who say is that not great, instead of passing 12 bills in a given period of time, they have passed 13 bills in that period of time. Does that in itself better serve the people of Canada? Are they not better served by perhaps one or two bills less being passed, since 85 per cent of them are passed unchallenged anyway. One Conservative member admitted to that earlier tonight.
If some of those bills are not passed because they are wrong, because the opposition indicated as much to the government, and because the people reacted, is that not better government? Is that not better for the people who sent us here? And is that not the reason why we were sent here, to serve our constituents, not to serve ourselves, or not to say when we retire or are defeated that under our particular stewardship, more legislation had been passed than the term before by some other government whose name the people will already have forgotten anyway? Is that not why we are here?

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
Together with my colleagues, I do not approve of these rule changes. We do not approve of the fact that this time today, at this crucial period in our history, was utilized for no other purpose than to change the rules. The purpose of the change in the rules, of course, is to make the government less accountable. We do not think that is a proper thing to do. We will not agree to them.
Even at this late hour, I still have a very cautious little bit of optimism in me that perhaps I can convince the government to repent and to do the right thing. Let me give it one more opportunity by asking it to vote at least for the following proposition.
Therefore, I move:
That the amendment be amended by deleting the number "21" and
adding after the words "proposed amendment numbered 24" the
following:
* 'and by substituting for the words " 11.00 o'clock p.m. " the words "12.00 o'clock midnight" in proposed amendment numbered 21".

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will recognize the hon. member for Chambly and have a look at the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to speak against the Standing Order changes. I would like to speak from my experience of coming here just a little over a year ago.
I came into this Parliament with the desire to serve my constituents to the best of my ability-
What a crock.

I hear the cynicism of the other side because they say: "What a crock". I do not believe that to be a crock and I do not think it is fair to myself. Neither is it fair to other members who sincerely believe they are here to represent their constituencies.
I would like to mention that I believe in this Parliament. Maybe some of the other members here on the government side do not. If we take a look at the changes to the Standing Orders, we would see that they do not believe in Parliament.
The reason we have these proposed changes is because the government wishes to shoot the messenger rather than change its practices. All we have done is brought out, as an opposition should, facts and figures showing
where the government has made mistakes. No government is perfect. This one surely is not perfect.
As a reward for what we have been trying to do as good parliamentarians, where we normally have 175 days where we would have Parliament convene, we have now 134 days if these changes are passed. This will seriously affect our role in the opposition and I even think the role of government members because I believe that when the government members are sitting here in Parliament they are much more responsible to their constituents and to all Canadians.
That does not have that much to do with Question Period, because I do not believe that there are any real questions asked that often in Question Period. Perhaps the minister on the other side would agree there are not always that many answers which are forthcoming either.
There are some things that do occur during Question Period which I find to be very productive. I will give you and example, Mr. Speaker, of some of those things, as one of my colleagues would know doubt have asked me, if I heard him correctly. One of those examples is that we are able to discuss things with ministers many times behind these curtains in a much more expeditious way than sending letters or memos. Many times we have a false impression of what the government is doing without making a statement in the House. We can find out from the minister exactly what is going on and save him some trouble and save us some trouble. That is what I call democracy. I think, Mr. Speaker, you can easily say that is what is serving your constituents best.
When we reduce the sittings of the House from 175 to 134, we reduce the opportunity of people like myself, parliamentarians, to directly speak off the record with ministers who are here and resolve issues which are important to people in our riding.
I can give an example. I can mention the Minister of Transport, for example. I never brought this up in the House before now because I did not feel it was appropriate.
Much to the credit of the Minister of Transport, I contacted him during the period when the House was sitting just after Question Period and informed him of a problem that they were having at Dorval airport where some of the taxi drivers were taking pay-offs in order to get the most lucrative trips.
April 11, 1991

The minister saw to it that the system would be changed and that those taxi drivers would be put out of that dispatch service. There was no big question in the House, and there was no major brouhaha. He just competently attacked the problem, and I thank him for it.
If the House sits less frequently, these types of opportunities to bring problems and situations to the attention of the Minister of Transport or the other ministers will not come up as often. It is very difficult when we are dealing with letters, secretaries and the minister's assistant to the assistant to that assistant. It is almost a kind of jungle that we have to cut through. It is unfortunate and should not be that way if we are all parliamentarians. I find it works very well.
There are people who listen as well on the government side, not always, perhaps, but frequently enough that if we can grab them after Question Period, things work out all right.
That is particularly why I am distressed with these rule changes. We will not have as much of an opportunity as we had in the past.
I am also concerned about the committee system because I like participating in committees. The reason why I like doing that is because we have more than a one minute question that we can ask. We can foul it up, and the minister who is there can foul it up. Many times we can discover things that we would not normally discover during Question Period.
I recall just today questioning the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I found it very interesting to learn that some of the people who were participating in writing a report on decriminalizing misleading advertising came from firms that had been guilty of misleading advertising. I never knew that, and the minister never knew that. He just found that out today.
That was not done in Question Period or in a press conference. That was done in the consumer affairs committee. I enjoyed that because it was informative and it was fun.
I am trying to think back to a committee that I found particularly enlightening. We are able to have one round of about 10 minutes when we can question the minister or any witness and we can follow it up with a second round of about five minutes. We can keep some flow and some continuity.
Government Orders
I think that is the kind of thing that the McGrath committee wanted to maintain back in 1985. He was a Conservative, but he wrote a very good report dealing with making parliamentary members more effective.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Housing); Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)
speechtext: What do you mean: "He was a Conservative, but he wrote a good report"? What is the inference?

My hon. colleague asked me about the inference when I said he was a Conservative but he wrote a good report.
The fact is that I have seen very few good reports coming from this government. I have seen some, but I have seen very few. I would be willing to say that as much as there have been some good reports, most of them have not been very good.
You are a socialist.

It is not a question of socialism.
If we take a look at the committee system as it stands now, it is a pretty good system. It works very well as far as getting information out and resolving problems.
When we have the committee system as the changes propose we can only call technical witnesses. What is a technical witness? What is a technical witness supposed to do when we require information from someone such as a minister or minister's assistant, a consumer's group or a group that is responsible for helping to write a regulation, a standards making group. These people have a lot of information to give. To have a committee which can only call technical witnesses is unfortunate and it would really gut the committee system.
That is unfortunate as well for people who are used to being called before committees, for consumer groups that have had a chance many times to tell committees what they have learned on the barricades, as I call it, or in the real world and for people who can come before government and explain their side of a story without being called socialists or without being called partisan in any way. I think we need more of that and that we do not have that much of it in this Parliament.
In addition, we add all the activities of the past year wherein the government has not been very respectful of members' rights to dissent. With respect to closure motions, even now we will be entertaining a closure motion when it is actually being debated before the courts. It seems at the minimum to be a contempt of court action because it is presently sub judice, but we are still engaging in closure.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
I do not really think that is fair. I do not think it looks good to the rest of the Canadian public because I think they would like us to be here as well as in our ridings and, when we are here, to earn our money. I do not think we will be earning our money by reducing up to 20-some per cent of the time we are here when we should be here and we are reducing that time.
I have just one final remark. The government should understand that we in the opposition are only trying to better serve our constituents. We are only trying to make this place work correctly. By protesting these rule changes we are not trying to score cheap political points. We understand that there is a majority over there with this government. It is a majority which is abusing its majority status to stifle dissent, to stifle any information that can come in from our side which could help the government and particularly to prevent independent groups from having their views presented before a committee of Parliament.
Having been here only a year and having had to work much of my time in my riding because the former member from my riding was not there that often, I appreciate the chances I have when I do come here actually to participate in all the committees and in the House.
The problem is one of what kind of participation. Should we just sit here as a government would obviously want us to do and nod our heads in agreement? We cannot do that, not when the government is wrong, but we can do that when the government is right. However, there are other more meaningful things that we should be able to do in the committees as well as in Parliament.
My minister friend on the government side pipes up occasionally whenever I try to be generous with his side. I wish he would just perhaps open his ears sometimes and understand that I am not trying to score points with him or with the government. I am just simply trying to say things as I see them and to present in a matter of fact way or in a common sense way why these rules changes are going to work against the rights of the constituents that we are supposed to represent.
I do not think that there is an urgency to pass these rule changes right now. I believe that the system is not broken. There is no need to fix it. There is no urgency. There are a great deal of other problems that Canadians are expecting us to tackle. If we were to make a list of things that our constituents would want us to deal with, I believe that probably the economy would be number one. Perhaps the Constitution would be down to number five or six. Obviously unemployment would be very high up. Yet our constituents, Canadian voters who are watching us now, are a bit mystified as to why we are talking about rules changes and democracy and what they have to do with their everyday existence.
It has to do with democracy. It has to do with their representation either directly before committees or to this government through their elected representatives, those of us on the government side as well as those of us on the opposition side.
When these people see us on television discussing something into the wee hours of the morning-because I suspect we are going to be here that long-I am embarrassed that we have to be spending that time on a subject which seems to be of such arcane interest. Really, there are better things we could do with our time.
We won't sleep.

My colleague says that we will not sleep. I do not think we will have time to sleep. We have some interesting debates coming up later on.
Why not look at the other issues before we look at changing the Standing Orders? Why do we have to deal with this right now? Surely there are enough things on our plate with which to deal without having to bore to a certain extent the viewers and listeners with what the government has imposed upon us.
We will probably have three or four more hours of debate. Then the government will just cut it off. That is very typical of this government.
They say that it is part of democracy, just as ramming through the GST, cutting off debate and cutting down the committee system. Yet, what did they do when a Conservative fellow presented a good report dealing
April 11, 1991

with the committee system back in 1985? I knew Mr. McGrath personally.
We are improving it.

I do not believe they are improving it. I believe that when we have this House management committee, for example, it will actually decide which committees meet. That strikes at the very heart of the McGrath report which wanted the committees to have as much independence as possible.
I am not going to go into all the jargon of why this is wrong. Most people will see that it is wrong and that this government has had a very bad year. It is reeling from its almost single digit polling result and desperately wants to cut off dissent. Temporarily this government will be able to reduce dissent, but it will not be able to cut it off.
It is all the more surprising-I remember watching television-when the Conservative Party was storming the Chair, complaining about its rights being abused, making the bells ring, engaging in all sorts of extra-parliamentary and parliamentary opposition. It was kind of guerrilla warfare. Today, when that party is in government, the hypocrisy is that it is doing exactly what they accused the Liberals of doing for so long, and that is what I call hypocrisy.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have had an opportunity to look at the amendment to the amendment and I find it in order.

Mr. Speaker, I am really pleased to take part in this debate. We all know the Government House Leader has tabled a motion to amend the Standing Orders of the House of Commons, after a series of fruitful discussions with members of all parties-Liberals, New Democrats and Conservatives. The series of reforms includes in particular changes to the schedule and to the Standing Orders of the House of Commons so that it can do business more expeditiously. I would like to give a few statistics about changing the parliamentary calendar.
The present parliamentary calendar provides for 175 sitting days. The average number of sitting days in 1991 is 155. The new calendar provides for 134. The calendar always provided for an average of 155 days or 881 hours a year. The new calendar provides for 134 days or 897
Government Orders
hours a year. I would like to mention how many days other legislatures sit. Let us take provincial and territorial governments for a period of three or four years: the Yukon Territory, 39 days; New Brunswick, 42 days; Prince Edward Island, 45 days; the Northwest Territories, 51 days; Newfoundland, 59 days; Nova Scotia, 62 days. Alberta, 73 days; Quebec, 74 days; Saskatchewan, 79 days; Ontario, 84 days; British Columbia, 89 days; Manitoba, 98 days.
I could also give some statistics for Canadians who often ask us for figures, especially my constituents. Australia, as my colleague from Laval-Est has said 77 days in 1991. The U.S. House of Representatives sat 144 days, or 814 hours, a year on average from 1961 to 1989. In the United Kingdom, they sit 170 days on average.
Mr. Speaker, the new schedule will enable members to divide their time better between their parliamentary obligations and their obligations to their constituents, thus meeting their constituents' desire for more direct contact with their member of Parliament.
Although the reform provides for fewer sitting days, the number of hours per day will increase.
The situation today is very different from what it was when the Standing Orders of the House were written. These days, members are asked to be in their ridings more often and on the other hand, Parliament requires more of them.
The changes made to committees respond to members' desire for a better adapted and more efficient structure of standing committees and a clearer distinction between standing and legislative committees.
The committees of the House will belong to one of five categories, each with four or five standing committees and two legislative committees. Members will thus be able to hone their knowledge in areas covered by the various committees in a given category, because the substitution rules will be more flexible.
The proposals also contain a provision to allow cameras in committee meetings with the approval of a majority of members. The government proposes that the House of Commons accept the recommendations from the Committee on Privileges and Elections regarding the process for Private Members' Business, which will en-

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
able ordinary members to present more bills and motions.
Mr. Speaker, Parliament's task is to debate issues and to make decisions and the Standing Orders of the House guide this process. They govern the proceedings of the House and establish a framework in which the government carries out its legislative program and the opposition holds it accountable. They were designed so that Parliament could do business in an orderly way and members could debate issues and make decisions by majority vote.
The modification to the Standing Orders before Parliament is the result of a year of discussions and great co-operation among the House leaders. It is the most important series of changes proposed in the modern history of the Canadian Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, with the proposed schedule, the House will sit on average 134 days per year, as opposed to an average of 155 days over the past 10 years. But the members are expected to sit approximately the same number of hours during the year. The changes to the schedule will give the members, especially those from the West and the Northwest Territories as well as from Northern Quebec and Ontario, more flexibility in planning the time they can spend in their riding. Government policies and legislation are more complex and Canadians show an interest in an increasing number of issues.
While the opposition can use an attendance reporting system and not have to worry about keeping most of its members in Ottawa these changes will help all members to fulfill their obligations in Parliament and their ridings, so that both Parliament and constituents receive all the attention and services they deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I listened to the speech the hon. member for Manicouagan made today about the difficulty of serving a huge riding. The riding of Manicouagan covers
450.000	square kilometers. My riding of Abitibi covers
550.000	square kilometers, with a population of 85,000, and it is hard indeed. We spend a lot of time here, in Ottawa. As my records show, and the hon. members are welcome to check, I am often present during the week, but when the week-end comes, we leave on Friday evening, spend Saturday and Sunday working in our riding, then come back to Ottawa. We have huge ridings.
For many summer is a time for hollidays. But we Northerners head out North, in Northern Quebec, in particular in the Nunavik area, to visit the Inuits and Crees and work with them to find solutions to their problems. It is the same thing for the member for Manicouagan, because we cannot get away when the Parliament is sitting.
The opposition parties are fortunate. Both the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party had their leadership convention in the past few years. We know there is a secret pact between them. It is rumoured in town and at home. It is a "one third, one third, one third" system. We saw it in action today, during the vote. There is one political party in this House that I will not mention which had only 18 members present out of 44 tonight to vote on this important motion. However, another party opposes the rule changes and that is the Liberal Party. Today, out of 81 Liberal members, only 44 were present. Mr. Speaker, with the "one third, one third, one third" system, we notice which members are often in Ottawa. We look across the room and wonder where the members have gone. We know why that is. They spend two weeks a month in their riding, and as many as three in some instances, because they do not need to stay here, so they can travel. Now they refuse a change which would give us, the members from large ridings, the opportunity to spend a week in our ridings to meet with our constituents.
Earlier today, I heard the member for Hamilton East say that we had met, that is true, on our way to the Senate for the royal assent and that I told her that I would be happy to go and spend one week per month in my riding for a working holiday. Upon our return to the House, she forgot the word "working" and mentioned only the word "holiday". That is pure partisanship! But when she went away for the leadership convention, she was away for a long time. It was not mentioned in the House at the time, but now we can pursuant to the rules.
Mr. Speaker, it is very important that we spend one week per month in our ridings. When I go back to my riding on Friday night, 50 weeks or so every year, I often work Saturday morning and afternoon to meet with my constituents or travel up North. I sometimes drive 400 or even 800 kilometers in one day and a half during the week-end to Matagami or Lebel-sur-Quevillon. I have a huge riding.
April 11, 1991

Government Orders
That is why we must have the opportunity to return home because it is important. Therefore, I will vote in favour of that motion, those amendments.
There is another thing that I would like to say to you. The other day, I noticed that three opposition members, three liberal members were away on a trip to Taiwan in the middle of a budget period, when it was most critical to be here if they wanted to take the government at task for that budget. But they chose rather to accept the invitation of Taiwan Chambre of Commerce to go there, all expenses paid. In other words, during the budget debate, those three liberal members, and I would like to mention the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell most specifically, who were here today criticizing the government and saying how important it is to be in Ottawa, were absent that very week.
Mr. Speaker, I have another thing to say to you, namely that your servant the member for Abitibi and several of my colleagues from the province of Quebec want to obtain the privilege that Liberal and NDP members already have to go away one week a month. I will vote for these amendments, for the people back home, for the population of Abitibi.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate for the second time this evening, especially after the speech by the hon. member for Abitibi. I must tell the House that it is the fourteenth time this government has cut off debate on government bills or motions in this House since the 1988 election.
It is absolutely horrible, Mr. Speaker, that a government can be so-what is the word?
Ridiculous!

Ridiculous, yes, that is possible, ridiculous by moving this motion once again. I am sorry to hear it and after rereading the details of the closure motions that the government has brought in this House, I am proud to take the floor to denounce the government for it.
Mr. Speaker, at the end of my speech in this debate yesterday, the hon. parliamentary secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada asked a question during the period for questions and comments.
He said:
I would just like to ask the member, who understands rules and procedure veiy well, why he chose to give us a history lesson instead of dealing with the technical difficulties he sees in the rule changes. Why would he do that when we are debating rule changes, and he does not deal with that?
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member is not here tonight. I hope that he is watching the debate on television; otherwise he may read it tomorrow in Hansard.

Perhaps I could switch to the other official language. The hon. parliamentary secretary is really going to miss something because I want to go through the details of the changes that the government has proposed to the Standing Orders. Before I do, I want to say something about the use of closure by the government.
The government has given notice of closure. It gave notice of closure yesterday and so we are debating this motion under the closure rule. As of the end of yesterday, 13 hours and 9 minutes had been spent discussing this motion. One hour and 58 minutes of the time spent on the discussion was spent by the Speaker having to read the motion out to the House. We can thank the members of the New Democratic Party for their great co-operation and brilliant tactics in forcing that rather childish episode on the House. They insisted that the Speaker read this motion instead of waiving the right, dispensing as we call it here, of the reading in order to delay the House and obstruct the proceedings of this House. They really should be hiding their heads in shame at this particular moment for that tactic. It was really childish and silly.
However, take that away and we have 11 hours of debate on this motion and the government is up on its hind legs proposing closure. The parliamentary secretary to the government House leader, who is the mastermind behind this scheme, knows perfectly well he put the deputy House leader up to it, and after a very reasonable speech, the poor hon. gentleman went off giving notice of closure in another disgraceful episode, number 14 in this Parliament. Who knows how many more times we are going see it because the government has indicated clearly that its view is that matters should be debated for a very brief time.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
So we had basically 11 hours of debate on a major set of rule changes. The Minister of State for Privatization yips away over there that there was lots of consultation. Sure there was lots of consultation, but it never went to a committee. Every major rule change that we have ever had to deal with in this House is a product of a committee report and this one is not. It is the first time the House has been subjected to major changes, certainly in the last 34 years, without a major committee report.
I want to go back to 1969.1 mentioned this debate the other day in the course of my speech when major changes that imposed the time allocation rules in this House were adopted. That debate went on for 12 days: July 8, 9,10,11,14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 22 and 24, 1969. Closure was moved on the 24th. There were a total of 38 hours of debate before the debate came to an end on that particular change of rules. What a contrast.
Here we have a government which has no particular legislative agenda at the moment, is in no need to rush us out of this House and yet is just absolutely convinced that the only way it can continue to run the country is to get the members of the opposition out of Ottawa, close this place down and get us away so that it does not have to listen to the criticisms of its dreadful policies.
They want to avoid Question Period.

They want to avoid Question Period, they want to avoid criticisms of their policies, they want to avoid everything.
Let me turn to the rule changes themselves. This may be a little technical and perhaps a little tedious, but I think it might be helpful, particularly to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General who was clearly very unhappy that I did not go through this the other day. So, to please him, I am happy to do so.
The first thing in the rule changes that we have opposed, and is opposed in our amendment, is the schedule that the government has suggested: three weeks on and one week off. I do not want to claim that it is always three and one; in some cases there are four weeks on and one away; fives weeks on and one away; and occasionally six. But there is clearly more time away than has been the case in the past. The number of sitting days is reduced to 134 from 175.
As members of the opposition we object to that. We feel that Parliament should be here more, not less, so that criticisms of government policies can be made, so the opposition can do its duty in calling the government to account. That is our principal objection to the policy.
We acknowledge, and I think that all hon. members will acknowledge, that more time with constituents is not in itself a bad thing and, indeed, many of us are quite happy to spend time in our ridings. But we were elected to serve in this House. We feel that is our primary obligation and we are prepared to meet that obligation.
Second, the government is proposing a change in the rules relating to petitions. Instead of unlimited time for their presentation, the government has put a maximum of 15 minutes on them. I have got to point out that if you take a quick look at the statistics for the period from April 1989 to February of this year, that is almost a two-year period, the average time per day on presentation of petitions in this House was eight minutes. Yet the government was so offended by members presenting petitions, because of course the petitions were so damaging to the government and its dreadful policies, that it felt it had to put a limit on it so we could not obstruct government business. It has insisted on a 15-minute time limit on petitions. That is the change in the rules in relation to those.
Then there is the issue of quorum. The quorum of this House at 295 members is 20 and it has been 20 for years and years, in fact since 1867. The House has grown in size since 1867 but the quorum has not increased. Yet this government with 160-odd members-it has had some defections I know, people are jumping off like rats from a sinking ship-cannot maintain a quorum in this House. In fact, the government decided that what it would do is change the quorum rules so that if there is a loss of a quorum on a day, instead of losing the item of business and having to reinstate it with a vote the next day, it would simply automatically have it go on to the Order Paper. That is the rule it has proposed and which we have suggested should be excised from this package. In other words there is no particular damage done if a quorum is not here on a particular day.
The only time there has been a lack of quorum in this Parliament was one Friday, a supply day. There was a quorum call and the government pulled all its members. The government Whip thought he would pull a trick. He said: "This is an opposition day", little realizing that opposition days are devoted to government business, the business of supply. So he pulled all his members and had them stay in the lobby. They did not come in and the House was adjourned for the want of a quorum. There they were on Monday morning with no business of supply on the Order Paper, and they looked so stupid. They were clearly embarrassed. The Whip was red-faced. The government House leader was embarrassed. He had to
April 11, 1991

move the business of supply again and have a vote and put it on the Order Paper. It took up about an hour of time.
I can understand why they would want to change the rule after such a humiliating experience, but it was generated by their own folly. It was an unbelievable exercise.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: It actually happened?

It actually happened and it was their own stupidity and they blamed the opposition for that. They say: "The opposition is calling quorum on us all the time. Why should we have to keep 20 members in the House?" That is the argument they are putting forward. They have 160. Surely it is not too much to expect 20 of them to be here.
Then they have cut back on the throne speech. Eight days debate on the throne speech was too long. Since I was elected in November, 1988, we have not completed more than one throne speech. We had a throne speech in December 1988 for the short session that dealt with free trade. We debated it for a day and went on to the free trade debate and that was that. We never went back to it. The session of Parliament was prorogued. Then the second session started and we had a full eight-day debate on that. Apparently eight days was too long for this government. Their members obviously were not interested in discussing its policies because after all it is government policy that is announced in the throne speech.
But there wasn't much in that speech.

The hon. member for Saskatoon-Dun-dum says: "You can't blame them. I wouldn't want to debate the policies either. They are such a disaster".
Nevertheless, at least from their point of view, what they did was say that they want to cut that back; eight days is too long; six days will do. And so there is the rule change.
They did exactly the same thing with the budget, so I do not have to repeat myself; six days reduced to four.
Government Orders
"We do not want to debate the budget too long, it is too embarrassing. The opposition is able to turn up too many problems, too many bad policies in our budgets if they are allowed to debate for six days. We will cut them back, we will cut it down to four days."
It was exactly the same thing with supply days. To have 25 supply days in a year is too many. The opposition can raise 25 embarrassing subjects; 25 embarrassing debates. The government looks stupid, the government looks incompetent, the government looks like it is blundering. They say: "We do not want that; we want to look good. So if we do not have those debates, we can introduce our own bills and discuss those instead. We will not look quite so bad". That is the attitude of the Tory government and that is what it has done. It has cut the supply days from 25 back to 20.
Then there is the closure rule. They moved closure tonight. I see the hon. member for North Vancouver, the chairman of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, does not enjoy my speech. I can understand why. He must find this very embarrassing. He should have had these rules referred to his committee. Then we would have had a decent discussion and had some public input on it. Unfortunately, his government would not co-operate with him to get them referred to committee. I am sorry he was unable to achieve that.
Curtailing debate or closure. Here we have a closure rule imposed on us today under Standing Order 52. For years and years and years, I think since the 1920s, the time for the adjournment on a closure debate was one o'clock in the morning. And so we will go until 1 a.m. or very close to it, tonight. But now the government says: "Oh, no, that is too late for our members. We cannot expect them to be in the House of Commons at 1 a.m. even if we choose to impose closure". It should be an inconvenience to the House to impose such a Draconian rule as the closure rule, but not to this government. It said: "No, we will just change the rules and move the time back to 11 p.m. It is much easier to finish at 11 p.m. That will make a shorter debate, and we do not mind cutting the debate back, cutting the opposition off on its chances of chastising and condemning our disastrous policies". So the government cut it back by two hours.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
The hon. member for Ottawa Centre says, quite correctly, they should blush for that, and I quite agree.
Then we have the time allocation rule. The government decide that time allocation rules are too generous. What is the rule now, for those on the other side who have forgotten? The rule is that if they cannot get agreement with the opposition, they may propose a motion to limit the time for debate. The motion is debatable for two hours and thereafter the government may allow within the motion for not less than one full day of debate.
The government has cut away the two-hour debate. That is gone. No two hours of debate to condemn the government for moving time allocation. Then the additional day can be the same day it proposed its motion In other words, it has saved itself 24 hours out of the time allocation process. It has become a more Draconian rule than it was before.
How many times has the government used time allocation in this Parliament? Eight times. Fourteen times for closure, eight times for time allocation. Twenty-two times it has cut off or curtailed debate in the course of this Parliament. It is a record. No government ever before has been this Draconian in its treatment of Parliament, this high-handed in its treatment of this House.
Then we turn to curtailment of debate on third reading of bills. What was the previous rule? The first member speaking for the government had unlimited time. The second member speaking from the opposition had unlimited time, and thereafter all members had 20 minute speeches with 10 minutes of questions and comments. What is the new rule? It is 40 minutes for the government, 40 minutes for the opposition, five hours of time with 20-minute speeches and then 10-minute speeches thereafter with no questions or comments. That is the new rule, shorter, curtailed debate. Limit the opposition, cut them off, make everything squeezed up so it happens faster. We are not going to have any protracted debates anymore on second or third reading of any government bill because this government is trying to shut the opposition up. That is the effect of its rule change.
As the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex says, it is the suppression of democracy.
Finally, we have the borrowing bill.
After cutting the budget debate from six days to four, it then proposed to limit the debate on the borrowing bill to two days. Everyone knows the borrowing bill is the government's instrument by which it borrows billions and billions of dollars from the Canadian public. It gives the government the authority to borrow this money.
