Clearly, it is a bill on which members may want to speak and address the general financial policies of the government. It is considered an extension in many cases of the budget debate, but it does not have to be. It could be moved on its own.
Yet, this government has included a rule that limits debate on the borrowing bill at second reading to two days. There is no need for closure or anything. It is just two, short, ordinary days in this House.
In this pile of changes, every single one is designed for one purpose; that is, to reduce the opportunities to the opposition to participate and criticize the government in this House. I know that every change on its own is relatively minor. The parliamentary secretary knows what I am saying is true. I know he wants to agree with me, but he is reluctant.
If he agreed with me, he would be in the Prime Minister's bad books. What we have here is a situation where each of these small changes, minor perhaps in itself in each case, adds up to a significant and substantial curtailment of the rights of the members of this House, particularly those in the opposition who want to criticize the government.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General wanted a detailed explanation of the changes. I hope that the speech I have given tonight has explained those changes in detail. Each of the changes I have listed was contained in the original amendment that we proposed to the government motion. We are asking that the government consider adopting this and scrapping those particular changes.
The others, we can live with. We do not like them all, but we can live with them.
There is one other that we have offered a change on. The subamendment that has been moved tonight is on the closure rule. We are willing to compromise.
Again, I hope that the parliamentary secretary will go out into the lobby to plead with the Prime Minister to make a change in this in particular and agree to the subamendment. Instead of ending the closure debate at one o'clock in the morning, we have agreed to move it
April 11, 1991

back to twelve o'clock midnight in order to help the government along and give us at least one extra hour of debate over what it is proposing.
I know that the parliamentary secretary does not mind staying up until midnight. I am sure he could convince some of his colleagues to do the same. Then, perhaps we would have at least the opportunity to get one additional hour when the government, on its own volition-and only a minister of the Crown can do this-moves closure.
It is a government initiative. If the government chooses to use closure, surely it is the one that should know it has to be here until 1 a.m. Not this government. It wants to end it at 11 p.m. We are prepared to compromise. We will saw off at 12 p.m. and carry on in that way. I think it is a reasonable compromise. I hope that the parliamentary secretary will deal with his colleagues and convince them of the rightness of our thoughts.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the hon. member's time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely pleased to participate in this important debate.
After 25 years in this House, I feel I have some insight into the value of the rules and the purpose of those rules in attaining the goals of Parliament.
If we are going to evaluate these proposed rule changes that are before us, we have to evaluate them alongside the traditional goals of Parliament to see if the rules are appropriate in meeting those goals.
What are the goals of Parliament that have been pretty well agreed to by experts over the years? We must remember that Parliament, as a body, is now over 700 years old. It developed in. Britain and in other Commonwealth countries as time went on.
The principle purpose of Parliament is, first of all, to scrutinize legislation. I say that in recognition of the fact that most legislation-about 90 per cent-that is presented in this House is presented by the government. It is only a small percentage that is put forward by the opposition because that is the way things work.
Government Orders
The government controls House time. One of the most important roles of Parliament is to scrutinize the legislation of the government.
Another important role is to scrutinize the administration of the government, whether the government is administering this country and the legislation of this country in an efficient way, in a sensitive way, in a way that is appropriate and meets the needs of the Canadian people. That is another important role.
A third important role of Parliament is to scrutinize the spending programs of the government. There is much concern in the country today about the large deficit, the large national debt, as to whether money is being spend wisely or not. Another important role of Parliament is to scrutinize the spending programs of the government.
Fourth and probably last is the role in scrutinizing new taxation proposals. Of course we went through a lot of that last year in attempting to scrutinize the government's proposals for the new GST, goods and services tax.
How do we go about doing the scrutinizing? We do it through debate by presenting opposing views, by picking holes in the legislation, by asking the government to explain. However, and this relates to one of the changes proposed by the government, in order to properly scrutinize long complex legislation-and legislation today is often long and complex; the bill on the goods and service tax was very long and complicated-it takes time.
As I said over and over again, the debate in this House is not necessarily to convince members on the other side of our arguments. The purpose of debate in this House, especially through the use of the media and television, is to convince the Canadian people of our arguments, to make an impact on public opinion outside this House. Then the public can go back and say to the government: "Look, we know you have a big majority in Parliament, but through the debate in the House of Commons we see that there is weakness in that legislation. We see that that legislation is bad for the Canadian people. We want you to change it". Then maybe you do get changes.
We have seen changes in legislation over the years because public opinion was aroused, but you cannot

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
bring matters to the attention of public opinion if you are only going to have a one-day debate or a two-day debate or if you use closure over and over again so that you do not really get into the subject matter of legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I must say-and you would know this because you have been here a good deal of time yourself-that very often it is only after the second or third or fourth look at a piece of complicated legislation that you see new aspects, that you see things you did not see the first time that could be very harmful to the Canadian public.
We do the scrutinizing, first of all, through debate. We do it by proposing amendments. That means we must have sufficient time to propose amendments. We do it through questions in the Question Period. We do it through questioning after the various speeches of members in this House. A good reform was brought in a couple of years ago which allowed for a 10-minute question period after each member's speech to make him accountable for the things that he said. Before we had that particular provision, members very often got away with saying all sorts of wild and silly things. Nobody could pick them up on it.
It is true that at that time we could beg the permission of the member to ask a question, but if he refused nothing could be done about it. Now it is written into the rules and that is a good thing. That is another way we hold people accountable for what they say.
We also do the scrutinizing of legislation, of administration, of spending programs and of taxes through the committee systems. In the committee system we are supposed to go into greater detail than we are able to do in this particular Chamber.
The other advantage of course that we have in the committees is that we can invite experts of all kinds to come in and comment on the legislation and can crossexamine them, and there is more informal procedure.
By this system, by these tools, we are supposed to do our job. I might say that Parliament has been able to do this more effectively when there are minority governments.
I know there are down sides on minority governments, but when we have minority governments-and on three occasions while I have been here we have had minority governments: in 1965, my first election, in 1972 and in
1979-the government is hostage to the House, has to respond to the elected representatives of the people, and cannot get away with ramming things through. They always have to get the agreement of one of the opposition parties and maybe two of the opposition parties.
In assessing these rules we cannot assume that we are always going to have majority Parliaments such as we had following the 1984 and 1988 elections; large majorities in both cases. But we have to make the rules, keeping in mind that we will also have minority Parliaments. If the political situation continues as it is today, according to the polls, we are likely to have a minority Parliament after the next election. Right now there are five parties in this country which are doing very well in the polls, and this could result in a minority Parliament.
I said there were down sides to minority Parliaments. Sometimes elected representatives of the people put pressures on the government that it does not like to have. On the other hand, it makes the government very responsive to the elected representatives of this country and every member counts, even on the government side. I was on the government side in minority Parliaments and more attention was paid to me then as a new member than much later when we had a majority, because they needed to convince me that every bill was right. They had to do that with all members of the House.
Another thing that is necessary in making Parliament effective is a proper flow of information to members of Parliament as opposed to government members. When I say "government members", I basically mean cabinet. If backbenchers on the government side and especially members of the opposition are going to properly lock horns with ministers who have huge public services to serve them in their departments-offices filled with assistants, researchers, economists, sociologists and statisticians-if we are going to properly challenge ministers, we need to have enough information on our side. That is why it is important that the committee system function properly and that we get the right experts before those committees.
It is also important that we have a properly financed and operating parliamentary library with a parliamentary research staff and that we also have enough proper staff in our offices. It means that members should have an opportunity to get back to their constituencies to talk with the people in their ridings in order to get feedback
April 11, 1991

Government Orders
on the different proposals put forward by the government.
I referred to the goals of Parliament and the tools we need to accomplish those goals. Now let us look at the rule changes being put forward by the government to see if it will really advance those goals or not.
In the first place they will reduce the number of weeks that we sit in a year by eight weeks. Parliament will sit eight fewer weeks than we do now according to these rule changes. What does that mean? It means that we will have 40 fewer Question Periods, 40 fewer times to question the ministers, to hold them accountable, to make them answer as to why they are doing this with respect to their administration and why they are doing that, why are they spending money this way or that way. We will have 40 fewer times to question the government in Question Period.
It also means we will have less opportunity to debate bills, to put opposing views, and less time to refer matters to committee. It is true that the committees might sit when the House is not sitting, as they do now, but things have to be referred to committees.
From my experience what happens when we shorten the timetable of the House. I said I allow for the fact that we need sufficient time in our constituencies, but I think this is going too far. That particular measure to shorten the parliamentary timetable so that we sit fewer weeks does not help us accomplish the goals of Parliament.
Next, these new proposals before the House would shorten the specialized debate and shorten the budget debate. The budget debate now, according to the rules, should go for at least six days. It would shorten that to four days. The speech from the throne debate, in which we discuss the general policy of the government, would be shortened from eight to six days; again less time for members of this House.
One must remember that this is a very large country from Victoria, British Columbia, from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland, from Windsor to the Northwest Territories, and that there are problems which differ from region to region.
The fact that maybe 10 Liberals are able to speak and 5 NDP members are able to speak does not mean that we have a proper view with respect to legislation. Of the 10 or 15 Liberals who might speak 5 may come from Ontario, 2 from Quebec, and there may be only 1 or 2 from the outer reaches, from the Atlantic area or from the west.
Because of the kind of country we have, we need those eight days to debate the general policy of the country. We need those six days to debate the budget, which has impacts in various parts of this country and on different communities.
Also, they would reduce opposition days from 25 to 20. Let me explain for Canadians who do not quite understand. How we spend the time in this House is decided by the government. Except for the Question Period each day when we are allowed to ask questions for 45 minutes, the government decides whether it is going to call bill a, bill b or bill c. If it wants to avoid a controversial measure it can very well do so. For example, if it has found that bill a has provoked a lot of criticism in the country, it can avoid it altogether and call bill b and it can then call bill c.
The opposition, although the government consults with the opposition, has no power in determining government bills, the business debated in the House. In order to compensate for that, we have had 25 opposition days where the opposition can decide on the subject matter to be debated whether or not it is embarrassing to the government. On some of those opposition days we can demand a vote of confidence or just a vote on the subject matter of the opposition motion.
The government is going to reduce that from 25 to 20 days. Again, how does this meet the goals of Parliament as I described them? Next it will cut the length of speech time. For second and third readings of bills, after five hours the time would be cut in half, from 20 minutes to 10 minutes. Mr. Speaker, and you would know this as an experienced member of this House, there are many issues that you cannot deal with in 10 minutes.
I can recall very well, in trying to put the arguments forward with respect to the abolition of capital punishment, that there was no way that I could deal with all the arguments for that particular controversial measure and at the same time in my speech deal with the arguments

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
raised against so that I could rebut those arguments. There is no way one can do it in 10 minutes.
I know that we have had 10-minute speeches at the end of debates for a certain time, but this is going much further. As I say, it will restrict members of the House to properly scrutinize the government's legislation, to properly scrutinize its administration, its spending program and its taxes. Again, I do not see how that change meets the goals of Parliament.
The government is also putting forward new rules that would facilitate the use of the guillotine. The guillotine is another type of closure, a way of closing off debate. I have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and the Canadian people that this government has used closure and the guillotine more since 1984 than it has been used by all governments since Confederation. Since 1984 it has closed down debate by the use of closure and guillotine more from 1984 to this date in 1991 than was the case from 1867 to 1984.
On many occasions we only had two or three days of debate on very important bills. Then I can remember in the committee on the unemployment insurance bill, which was again a massive social change for this country, the government put closure on the length of time the committee could sit and listen to witnesses. Of course, we had to turn down many people and many groups who wanted to participate in that discussion because they were going to be hurt very much by the cutbacks to the unemployment insurance system.
As my colleagues have said, there are some positive things in these rule changes. On the whole, the purpose of these changes are to cut back the rights of Parliament, and in particular the opposition, in scrutinizing legislation. It also hurts the government backbenchers. If we sit less, we have shorter speeches. A government backbencher wants to put on the record the views of his area, of his constituency or of his region with respect to a bill, whether he comes from northern Ontario, Cape Breton, northern Saskatchewan or from a big city like Vancouver. He may not have the opportunity to do so and, if he does get the opportunity, he only has 10 minutes. It not only hurts opposition members but it also hurts government members. They will learn it because they may very well be in opposition after the next election. They will be extremely saddened by what they are trying to do tonight by the use of closure, again ramming through these rule changes.
The rules of Parliament traditionally have been developed by consensus. In this case that was not done. The rules of this place, unlike ordinary legislation because ordinary legislation can be divided along great policy lines, great philosophical lines, should be based on a consensus. It is not always easy to get unanimous agreement so it should be based on consensus.
I see that I have three minutes left. There are things that could be done which might radically change the face of this House and make it a really effective Parliament in which to do the sorts of things I referred to at the beginning of my remarks. I personally believe that if we change the rules so that a government could not fall unless there was a specific want of confidence motion or a specific motion put down by the Prime Minister that Parliament be dissolved, we would get amendments to legislation, improvements to legislation, which would be beneficial to the Canadian people.
If as members of Parliament both on the government side and on the opposition side we knew that we could sometimes defeat legislation without defeating the government, that we could amend government legislation without defeating the government, I think we would have better legislation. It would be an end to that old rule, that old tradition, that old convention we have that every time we defeat a government bill or we radically change a government bill the government must resign and seek a new election. I think the day of threat that the government has of dissolving Parliament if we do not support its legislation should be over. There should only be an election if the opposition very purposely puts a clear motion of want of confidence in the government. The government should only be able to dissolve Parliament if it puts before the House a motion to dissolve Parliament and go to the people.
It is true that if it has a majority it will easily pass that, but that is what we would be debating. For example, let me refer to the bill whereby the government decided to count as income for unemployment insurance severance pay and retirement income, which a lot of members on that side did not like as well. I can remember the member for Annapolis Royal and other members opposed the legislation. We would have been able to amend that legislation and make it better legislation. I think it would have been better for the government in the long run. The former Minister of Employment and Immigration lost her seat in Kingston basically because of that particular legislation. There were a lot of former public servants, members of the RCMP, of the correc-
April 11, 1991

tional service and so on, who just did not like that legislation.
There are many things that could be done. For example, with respect to the length of speeches, if we had a rule somewhat similar to that of the United States where at the end of your time-and let us say the time is 20 minutes as it is now-you had not finished your speech, you would be able to table a paragraph on the record to complete the speech. I think that would be very helpful.
I see that my time is up. Let me simply conclude by saying that most of these rule changes that are being proposed to this House will not help Parliament do the job that it is supposed to do for the Canadian people. This package of rules changes is just another knife in the back of democracy.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to be speaking on this motion in this debate. Within a couple of hours it is going to be arbitrarily passed, because of course of the motion of closure. This may very well mark one of the last 20-minute speeches that many of us will be making in this Parliament, including myself, as this legislation goes through.
There have been all kinds of references to the rules in this House, references to some of the more minor ones, references to some of them which are more profound.
I had a very interesting experience with some of the rules of the House in the wee small hours of the morning during the debate on the gulf war. I will get to that in a minute. I committed a breach, within a very short period of time, of two rules of this House which the present Clerk reminded me of at the time, and I thank him very much for that. Actually, if you break the rules once you get a warning, if you do it twice, there is a penalty. I will not go into a description of what the penalties are, but if anyone cares to ask me-if anybody is watching on television, as I am sure they are, they were certainly watching at 3.30 in the morning in the middle of January-what the penalties are I will be only too pleased to let them know.
On the surface of it, it would seem that those two rules were rather trivial and yet, if one looks at what they
Government Orders
represent in this House, they are very profound as well. The first rule I broke was to walk down the aisle between what was, at that time, Madam Speaker and the person who was speaking. I was reminded by Mr. Marleau of having broken a rule and I was not aware of it. After he mentioned it to me I was.
I was speaking to one of the Clerks at the table and the Clerk on the other side had the information which I was seeking. So I walked around to the other side of the table and I broke the second rule which was to walk between the Speaker and the Mace. There is a penalty for that too, although the first time is a warning. It seems rather trivial, but I think they are both the epitome of what this House is all about and why we have rules at all.
In the first case, I was extremely impolite. I had walked between the person who was speaking and you, Mr. Speaker, the symbol of authority in this House. In the second case, I walked between what is your symbol of authority and yourself. Both represent something which is of long tradition and which I really do believe sort of summarizes what this place is all about: civility, tradition and respect; respect for ourselves, respect for the job we have, respect for the House, respect for the people whom we represent and respect for the country of which we are all a part.
Of course, there is a reason for those rules beyond the respect for everything I have just mentioned. There is not an organization in the civilized world and certainly the parliamentary procedures, the general rules which we are talking about, whether they apply to your local hockey association or your local Rotary Club or the House of Parliament or what, do have such a civilizing and modifying affect on our behaviour. In a general sense, without going too far beyond, I guess the present context of this House, which is the British parliamentary system, many of the rules which we have adopted are part of tradition.
But what on earth is wrong with tradition? Someone mentioned that they thought it would be better if Mr. Speaker were to be wearing a suit as they do in the United States. Mr. Speaker, there are reasons why you wear what you wear and, without going into it, I think if anyone cares to realize what that is and the authority that it represents that is fine too.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
The basic assumption of all these things, whether it is in your local hockey club or in the House of Parliament, is that the majority shall rule and, within this House, we certainly recognize that those on the other side of the House have the majority. However, absolutely essential within that concept is also the necessity that the minority be heard. That is the bearing on which these rules have so much importance.
The rules of the House have evolved in this House and elsewhere to protect the rights of the minorities. It means that in the case of the opposition in the House of Commons, the rules have evolved, although I would suggest in the first four years of this government some extremely good changes were made. The McGrath commission made its report and some very good changes were made which made it much more possible for the minority, for the opposition in this House to be able to be heard.
I would suggest that if the major proclivities of the present government had been in effect at that time, there certainly would not have been those kinds of rule changes. A good proportion of what we are talking about right now is an attempt by this very same government to revert to the days before the McGrath commission, to take back some of the ability the opposition has, some of the ability which the minority in this country has to be able to express themselves and to be able to function in the manner which the tradition of the British parliamentary system has dictated the opposition should be able to do in order to protect the minorities within the country.
Probably one of the most significant things that has been said in this debate in so far as why the government would possibly want to make these changes came from some member opposite who said that it really was a shame that during Question Period it was primarily the opposition which was able to exercise any kind of activity during Question Period, that really it was an infringement upon the rights of the backbenchers of the government side, not to be able to get involved in Question Period.
That too is part of tradition. Question Period is not for the government. Question Period is not to give government backbenchers an opportunity to get involved. Question Period is an extremely valuable tradition which probably, on the basis of the proclivities of this present government, would never have been instituted in the British parliamentary system if all governments had thought this way. Sometimes, I guess, if you were on the government side, and even sometimes I wonder when I
am on this side, how on earth the parliamentary system ever evolved to the point where there was a Question Period.
What it signifies is that over time, through tradition, those who cared about the rights of people, those who cared about the rights of minorities, generously decided that yes, indeed, they would give the opposition the ability to be able to question the government. Certainly the parliaments of the world are far richer for that evolution having taken place and for that ability to have come about.
The very fact that someone in the government on the opposite side would even suggest-I do not know whether they are a member of the cabinet or not-that the backbencher should be able to be far more involved with Question Period, I think is symptomatic of how this government would really like to be able to throttle the opposition. It would like to control it and it would like to be able to cut it down.
In an attempt to do that, in addition to all the things it has have done since 1988 when I came to this House and of which we are all aware, it has used closure many times. In almost every instance, it has used closure so it is certainly no surprise that in ending this debate, it would be bringing in closure.
The very idea that the government would even have done that is so much in opposition to what this whole parliamentary system is about, that it should have brought in closure as many times as it did; that it would even suggest that there should be less of an ability of the opposition to debate things as they are now, which it is certainly doing within this legislation, is just something that I cannot understand. A government which five or six years ago brought in rather exemplary changes is now bringing in these kinds of changes.
This government, when in opposition, was able to ring the bells, holding up this House for 14 days over something with which it disagreed. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, and I will not speak for anyone but the New Democratic Party, but I suspect there may be other parties in this House who at the time of the introduction of free trade, of the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, of the GST, would probably on all those occasions and even more have willingly rung the bells for 14 days had we had the opportunity. But once these people got into power, ringing the bells for 14 days, holding the House up for 14 days for what they thought at the time was a good cause, and certainly what we
April 11, 1991

would have thought was a good cause, was not something they allowed the opposition any more.
The longest the opposition can ring bells now is for 30 minutes at any one particular time. That too gives us a comparison of how well the previous governments, how judiciously they viewed the ability of the opposition to function compared to what this government does. It is not any surprise that they have done this.
Some of the changes which they are proposing are changes to the calendar, where ostensibly we will be sitting for three weeks and having one week off. I am not convinced, in spite of all the arguments from the other side of the House that if these rule changes are brought in and that is one of them, that that is the way this House will conduct itself. At the present time we have a calendar. I do not know how long that particular calendar has been in effect in this House, but we have one. We are all aware of it. I do not think there has been any six-month period since I have been here when we have adhered to the calendar.
In 1987, at a time when presumably there was a similar calendar in effect, the government called the House back in emergency session to deal with an immigration problem in August. The House sat continuously until September 1988, in spite of what the calendar said.
I have a suspicion that in spite of all the fine arguments made on the other side of the House that this House at times will be sitting more than three weeks and may very well, despite the calendar, be away from this House for more than one week at a time.
Other changes being brought in are adjustments to business within the days of the calendar. There is a suggestion that the presentation of petitions will be limited to 15 minutes a day.
Previously someone else pointed out that on average the length of time taken for petitions has only been eight minutes a day anyway. I guess that is one change of which we probably ought to be glad and something of which we should be only too willing to take advantage. There are times, when presenting petitions from my constituents, I felt I really would like to be a little more explicit about their concerns. I am sure that the expansion of the length of time for presenting petitions to 15 minutes from the average eight is something that will be very welcome.
Many previous speakers have referred to the restructuring of the committee system. It is, again, just part of the government's methods of being able to limit the
Government Orders
ability of the opposition and of the minority to function as well as they have been operating up to this time, particularly since the implementation of the McGrath commission, with those changes having been made and the ability of the committees to function having been expanded by the government in a previous session of this Parliament. I suppose they are now backing off on that expansion.
I suppose the government members find that, in spite of the fact they thought it was helpful for the Canadian public to be able to function in a more democratic way, they themselves find it is not all that effective for them. I am sure it is an embarrassment for them when the committees do their work well. I was, myself, a member of one of the committees where that happened. When these changes go through that is something that will certainly not be able to occur as well within this House any longer.
There is a suggestion that only technical witnesses will be able to be heard. If we have a committee that is looking into the social problems of this land does that change mean that someone who is poor and who, I would suggest, would probably be one of the more technical witnesses a committee could possibly hear from, would be excluded because he or she is not a social worker?
Does this change mean that, if a committee were to examine a subject that concerned labour, they would not be able to bring a working person to the committee so that the members would be able to hear them? I would suggest that someone who is a working person and whose daily life is being affected by changes within the Commons ought to be heard by a committee and not only by the Minister of Labour or the Deputy Minister within the department.
There has been a suggestion that one of the only ways in which the Canadian public will be able to get their views across will probably be through the Senate committees because so far, at least, the government has not gone to the extent of limiting the ability of Senate committees to be able to hear witnesses and operate in a much freer way.
I am also told that the new system, which is certainly going to be passed here, will require fewer meeting rooms. I would suggest that perhaps, Mr. Speaker, through your good graces, you would put pressure on the government to re-establish the Reading Room, also part of the tradition of this House, presumably with fewer rooms being required. Perhaps the Reading Room could be restored to its original splendour.

April 11, 1991
Government Orders
I have already referred to reduced speaking time. This may be the last 20-minute speech that I will be able to give in this House for a considerable amount of time. It is worthwhile mentioning that, because I can remember that, when I was working on the legislation that changed the unemployment insurance, I had the opportunity to speak for 40 minutes on one occasion.
That sounds like a long time, but even that was an insufficient amount of time to be able to get the concerns of the people I was representing across the House to the government; namely, those who were going to become unemployed and those who find themselves restricted as far as employment is concerned. Certainly, the reduced amount of time is not going to be able to give the members an opportunity to represent themselves.
In conclusion, I see that my time is almost running out. The rule changes are not going to cure what is wrong with this House, which began in 1984 with this present government.
If the government really wants some changes in this House, let it listen to the people, as it has not done on almost every occasion. Listen to the people. The opposition will not have to be as strident or insistent in its work and this place will run much better.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker.

I like your tie.
Mr. Harb You like it, eh? Made in Canada. The hon. member likes my tie and I am willing to take it off right now and pass it on to him if he can convince his colleagues to retract their initiative in terms of the House sitting arrangement.
I stand to state my opposition to the government proposition to reduce the number of days we are sitting in the House for quite a few reasons.
First, I find it somewhat outrageous at a time when we have all those very different types of issues before us as a country, as a nation, that we are cutting down on the number of days we are spending here in order to do very important business for our country.
If we are to compare ourselves to the private sector, for example, any corporation, in the private sector, and if management is to make such a proposition, I can assure you that in that time that company will be out of business.
The difference between us and any private sector company, of course, is there is no one really out there to
measure the productivity of the House between elections. There are the people at large or the shareholders of the country who can measure our productivity around election time.
If the government is running out of subject matter, I might suggest a few tonight that the government can look at. It looked like it had run out of propositions, out of legislation and that is why it wants to cut down on the number of days.
I might suggest, for instance, for the government to look at the economy instance, and look at the possibilities of commitment to full employment at a time when we have over 1.6 million people who are unemployed. Look at the question of the high number of bankruptcies in our society. If we look at the western world and western nations, we are ranking pretty high out there. Look at some sort of an incentive encouragement to small business whereby we can encourage small employment and we can help small business to survive this tough economic time.
There are other questions such as the environment where the government can spend and continue with some sort of a commitment to deal with the issue of the environment, help clean up our rivers, our lakes and also to an extent the harbours in Atlantic Canada.
There is also the question that deals with national unity at a time when we are seeing the debate raging from coast to coast. I think it is only fair for us as parliamentarians to sit here and debate this issue seriously.
There is also the question of our social programs and the maintenance of our social programs. The latest statistic shows there are between 130,000 to 250,000 people who are homeless, who do not have homes. Finding a solution to that is only fair and it is something that the government should take very seriously and deal with it.
There is subject matter such as education and literacy at a time where we have high illiteracy rates, approximately 38 per cent according to the latest statistics, and the drop-out rate when it comes to our youth is approximately about 30 per cent which means, in other words, in our society nowadays for every 100 students who enter school, approximately 30 of those who drop out before the age of 18. That to me is a priority. It is a priority for our society and should be a priority for our House and for our government.
If my colleagues across tell me: "Well, we are running out of subject matter to deal with", these are a very few and I am sure if they are to provide the opposition parties with the time necessary, we can, in fact, help
April 11, 1991

them out even to draft legislation to deal with those issues.
The reason why we want to reduce the time that we are sitting here to allow MPs to go back to then-constituents and meet with them, I think, is a legitimate one, and I would have loved to have spent 100 per cent of my time with my constituents. But the fact of the matter is that we were elected to perform our duties inside of the House and also as well outside the House with our constituents.
Certainly there is a need to find some sort of a balance. There is no question about it. That is why we have constituency offices and capable staff in our constituency offices who can be our representatives at the constituency level. Of course some of my colleagues will say there is no substitute for a good MP. There is no doubt in my mind that might be right to a large extent, but people understand that we have a very important job to do here, and they expect us to be here.
I am also quite unhappy about the way it was handled. As my colleague mentioned a little earlier, the House is going to be limited to a maximum of 15 minutes a day to introduce petitions. To use the GST as an example, if we were to introduce all those petitions at once in the House of Commons it probably would have taken us quite a few days. My understanding is that in excess of 200,000 Canadians from all across the country signed petitions against the GST. They want the government to know about their views, and they expect their member of Parliament to present those petitions. I believe it is only fair to allow a member of Parliament enough time to introduce those petitions in the House.
As my colleague indicated, the average time it took in the past couple of years was approximately eight minutes. The time allocation of 15 minutes perhaps might not be a bad idea, but as an over-all arrangement I am against it because I do not think we should put a time limit on voicing the concerns of our constituents.
I could go on and state why the House should not be off for one week every four weeks. I basically get paid in order to serve my constituents. I would suggest my constituents and all of our constituents expect us to spend time in the House.
I truly believe that three years from now, when the Liberals form the government, my colleagues on the other side of the House will perhaps come back to haunt us by telling us: "We told you so". I am willing to take the risk and say: "Yes, but there is a price for democra-

cy". I truly believe that it is the wrong thing for the government to do at a time when perhaps we should look at every free bit of time to deal with the issues of the economy, the Constitution, the environment, education, illiteracy and so on.
After I have gone through this presentation, I hope my colleagues across the way will have a little meeting with the House leader and the Whip and come back here just before twelve o'clock and reverse their decision. Then we will go home happily.
